item.title: Why a ‘rise’ can be ‘meteoric’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Q: Why a “meteoric rise”? Meteors crash down on Earth.

A: The use of “meteoric” for something that rises may seem counterintuitive, but the adjective has been used that way for more than a century and a half, and the usage is standard English.

In fact, the usage ultimately comes from ancient Greek, where μετέωρος (meteoros), the source of “meteor” and “meteoric,” means raised or aloft.

Standard dictionaries define “meteoric” as relating to meteors or resembling them in speed or brilliance. All eight standard dictionaries we regularly consult use the phrase “meteoric rise” in their examples for the “speedy” sense.

Here are some examples: “a meteoric rise to fame” (Merriam-Webster, American Heritage): “His meteoric rise to stardom” (Webster’s New World); “her meteoric rise from dancer to professional actress” (Longman); “his meteoric rise in politics” (Dictionary.com), and “The group had a meteoric rise to fame in the 1990s” (Cambridge).

When “meteoric” first appeared in the early 17th century, it meant “relating to, or consisting of elements of, both the earth and the heavens,” according to the Oxford English Dictionary. The only OED citation for this obsolete sense is from a letter by John Donne to a friend, Sir Henry Goodyer, believed written in 1612:

“Our nature is Meteorique, we respect (because we partake so) both earth and heaven” (from Letters to Severall Persons of Honour Written by John Donne, Sometime Deane of St Pauls, 1651).

In the late 18th century, the dictionary says, “meteoric” started being used in referring to meteors or meteorites. It cites a satirical column in the Pennsylvania Gazette, Jan. 26, 1785, that compares current events to “a fiery ball” in the sky, then asks readers to pardon “this meteoric digression.”

In the late 18th or early 19th century, according to OED citations, “meteoric” began being used figuratively to mean “flashing or dazzling like a meteor, transiently or irregularly brilliant; rapid, swift; appearing suddenly.”

The first Oxford citation for the flashing sense is from “Cheerfulness,” an ode by the Irish poet Thomas Dermody, written sometime before his death in 1802: “His godlike hair, of braided rays, / His vest, a meteoric blaze” (from The Harp of Erin, Containing the Poetical Works of the Late T. Dermody, Vol. II, 1807).

The dictionary’s earliest citation for the speedy sense is from the Daily Chronicle (London), Jan. 16, 1895: “We had occasion to undertake a somewhat meteoric flight from Balmoral.”

However, we’ve found a much earlier example that includes the phrase “meteoric rise.” It compares the suddenness of Byron’s success as a poet to the “meteoric rise” of Napoleon:

“He called himself, in one of his poems, ‘the grand Napoleon of the realms of rhyme;’ and there is some similarity between the suddenness and splendour of his literary career and the meteoric rise and domination of the First Buonaparte” (from The Student’s Manual of English Literature: A History of English Literature, 1864, by Thomas B. Shaw).

The phrase “meteoric rise” is much more common than “meteoric fall,” according to Google’s Ngram viewer, but the falling usage does appear once in a while, as in this example about the decline of the moth Alabama argillacea:

“Ode to Alabama: The Meteoric Fall of a Once Extraordinarily Abundant Moth” (the headline on an article by David L. Wagner in American Entomologist, July 1, 2009).

item.title: administration and government
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

It's about time this topic has its own blog post. It's been an aside to other discussions on several occasions. It's not so much a difference between American and British English per se, but a difference in how our political systems work, and hence a difference in which words we need to use about them.

Because the UK has a parliamentary system of government, the political party that controls the parliament is the ruling party of the government as a whole. So, people talk about the Labour government or the Conservative government when that party has the majority of seats in the House of Commons, since that party chooses the person who will be prime minister, who then makes the political appointments to cabinet positions. Those people of that party are, essentially, governing.

The US has a presidential system, in which the president is elected independently of the legislature. The executive (presidential) and legislative branches of government are accorded their own powers, and the party in control of the executive branch may not be in control of either or both of the legislative chambers (the Senate and the House of Representatives). So when talking about the president and cabinet, it's inaccurate to say things like the Obama government (let me live in the past, please), since the president leads only one branch of the government. Instead, we usually speak of the Obama administration.

So, this isn't really a difference between AmE and BrE because if Americans talk about British politics, they would need the more parliamentary language, and if Britons talk about American politics, they'll need the more presidential language, for accuracy. But do people always speak accurately about these things?

For government, they mostly do. The images below show the most common words between the and government in the AmE & BrE parts of the Corpus of Global Web-Based English, which was collected in 2012–13, when the UK had a coalition government of the Conservative and Liberal Democrat parties. There, you can see coalition and Labour in the UK data, but only general adjectives and countries in the American. That hasn't changed in more recent data. There's little talk about the Biden government or the Trump government.

item.title: Wales coach Tandy frustrated by Australia defeat
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth analysis of the match and coach's perspective

Wales coach Tandy frustrated by Australia defeat

Wales head coach Steve Tandy said he was frustrated as his side failed to back up their epic win over New Zealand, narrowly losing to Australia.

The Wallabies edged the Nations Championship Test 29-26 in Cardiff, a week after a first Wales victory over the All Blacks since 1953 had led to wild celebrations.

Taniela Tupou, Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Max Jorgensen and Len Ikitau secured a try-bonus point for Australia as Ryan Lonergan and Carter Gordon added nine points with the boot.

Wales also scored four tries, through Dewi Lake's double, Blair Murray and Ryan Elias, with Sam Costelow landing three conversions.

However, they fell agonisingly short.

"The overarching feeling is the frustration of losing," said Tandy.

"We were disappointed. We probably weren't as accurate as we could have been. We were held up three times and could have gone ahead on the scoreboard."

Tandy added: "Maybe we needed a little bit of composure but there were enough opportunities to come away with the win.

"I know it's not the result anyone wanted but the supporters were amazing again."

Despite the loss, and that frustration, the Wales head coach praised his side's attitude in attempting to follow up their historic win against the All Blacks.

"Fair play to the boys, after such a monumental game last week with the emotional energy, we stuck in the game and scored four tries," he said.

"So there are a lot of positives in the performance to take as well."

Highs and lows of sport - Lake

Australia, having soaked up fierce first-half pressure, produced some fine attacking rugby after the break to prevent Wales from winning three matches in a row for the first time since the 2023 World Cup.

"It's sport, you have major highs and then lows, and that's the game we play," said skipper Lake.

"Our frustration comes from the fact that we probably weren't at our best.

"We created opportunities during large parts of the game, but there were little inaccuracies at the wrong times."

Lake, however, said he could not fault the effort of the squad.

"We spoke about backing up last weekend, and we didn't back it up with a result but I think we backed it up with effort and energy," said the captain.

"We had opportunities to win that game, but unfortunately it wasn't to be for us today.

"We'll fix those accuracy issues and we'll be ready to go again next week."

Wales will face Japan at the Allianz Stadium at Twickenham on Saturday after both sides finished fifth in the two Nations Championship tables - north and south.

It will be a fifth time Wales and Japan have met in 16 months with Tandy's side defeating Eddie Jones' team 28-21 in Cardiff just two weeks ago.

Wales have an injury doubt over scrum-half Tomos Williams who has a tight groin, with Tandy expected to make a number changes to freshen up the side.

Australia grateful for breaking losing sequence

Australia head coach Les Kiss was happy to have broken a four-match losing sequence which included recent defeats against Scotland and England.

"I am not only proud but also happy for these boys," said Kiss.

"The work they've been putting in over the last four weeks has been good and they just haven't been getting a reward

"Hats off to Wales. They beat the All Blacks here last week but didn't seem to lack any verve or energy.

"That didn't take it out of them and actually created more energy and confidence in them."

Captain Harry Wilson said it was a special to end the Wallabies poor sequence.

"When you have four losses on the bounce, you question a few things," said the back-row forward.

"Rugby is such a results-driven game and we hadn't been getting the results even though I felt like we weren't far off last week

"To beat a team who just had defeated the All Blacks, in front of 65,000 Wales supporters where the atmosphere was crazy, was special."

The Wallabies will now face Ireland on Friday in the contest for fifth place in Twickenham (20:10 GMT) after both sides finished third in their respective pools.

Source: BBC Sport | Published: 2026-11-22 04:50 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Champion’s corner: KC Current win first NWSL Championship with 2-1 stunner over Spirit
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Comprehensive coverage of the championship win

It took five years, 90 minutes and a goal for the ages, but the Kansas City Current have their first-ever NWSL championship.

Riding a wave of momentum created by a 54th-minute Olimpico from midfielder Vanessa DiBernardo, and capping it off with an all-important breakaway winner from Debinha, the Current silenced the partisan, sellout crowd at the heavily-favored Washington Spirit’s home ground with a 2-1 victory on Saturday.

The Spirit, heartbroken at the final whistle, have now lost three consecutive NWSL Championships.

“Obviously this one hates way worse than any of the other ones,” forward Trinity Rodman said afterward. “I don’t even think you have words in this moment — it is too fresh.”

DiBernardo’s goal was stunning, a driven, bent corner kick played to the far post that eluded Spirit goalkeeper Sandy MacIver, her defenders and Current forward Haley Hopkins, potentially DiBernardo’s intended target. The Spirit’s players and fans alike pleaded with center referee Joshua Encarnación, suggesting he examine the play on VAR for obstruction, as MacIver had potentially been screened. The review never came.

Whether played directly on goal intentionally or otherwise, the effort will go down as one of the most memorable in NWSL Championship history. At 34, DiBernardo becomes the oldest player in league history to score in a final, and was later named the match’s MVP.

The game’s early phases were forgettable save for one incident which would go on to affect the remainder of the match: a bruising, high-speed tackle on Rodman by Current defender Laney Rouse in the fifth minute. The challenge sent Rodman flying and appeared to injure her left elbow; the Spirit forward, nearing tears, spent much of the first half in visible pain and seemingly never fully recovered. Rouse was not cautioned for the challenge.

“[It helped set the tone] in the sense that it hurt really bad, yes,” Rodman said. “As a team, you always want to put the first hit in. You’re taught to do that. Credit to them. I wish I was the one who put her on the ground. They did a really good job at setting the tone and controlling the first half.”

It was far from the game’s only physical moment. Neither team managed to settle into any meaningful rhythm during an opening 45 that felt at times more like a title fight than a title match. Encarnación, involved in his first NWSL final, called a very tight match and the near-constant stoppages in play were the defining characteristic of a sometimes ugly opening phase. In many ways it was not entirely his fault: the message-sending start from KC and the Spirit’s subsequent response often compelled him to act. The 19 combined first-half fouls between both sides were the most in any half of any NWSL title match in league history.

“It felt like we couldn’t play more than two minutes without a whistle,” Rodman said. “We were fouling, they were true calls for sure — but I think you lose control of the game really quickly that way ... It definitely messed with our rhythm a little bit.”

Paradoxically, though, the match was won with speed. Deep into second-half stoppage time, the Current found their eventual match-winner on a breakaway. After doggedly winning back possession after a Spirit free kick late on, Kansas City forward Debinha streaked upfield from just beyond the center stripe, looking off a wide-open Temwa Chawinga and rounding MacIver who looked on hopelessly as the Brazilian slotted it home.

Moments later, Rodman – somehow still in the match after not only the early challenge but a later high-speed collision with Current goalkeeper Lorena – pulled one back for the Spirit. Falling away from goal 10 yards out, Rodman got her head on the end of a Tara Rudd cross, placing it perfectly over Lorena’s outstretched arms and into the far-side netting. The ensuing five minutes – the game ended in the 102nd – were chaotic but the Spirit couldn’t quite find the equalizer.

After a slow start, the Current were well-managed by former Major League Soccer and US national team member Chris Armas. Armas was widely considered a controversial selection at the time of his appointment but proceeded to lead the club to their first championship in his first season, doing so by beating Gotham FC and now the Spirit, two sides picked by many as potential league-winners.

“I think from the front to the back we made it a point that every person on this team defends and if somebody is going to make a mistake the other person is going to have their back,” Current defender Izzy Rodriguez said. “We try and turn every 1v1 situation into a 1v2 for us, and I think that showed up today. We were winning our duels and second balls and those are things that win games.”

For the Spirit, the loss is devastating. They become the first American professional club – men’s or women’s – to lose three consecutive finals since the New England Revolution of Major League Soccer, who did so in the mid 2000s. In their five Championship appearances, the Spirit have won just one time, in 2021.

Source: The Guardian Sport | Published: 2026-11-22 03:55 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

France book South Africa rematch in Nations Championship final with bonus-point victory over Argentina

France beat Argentina 45-17, securing the bonus-point victory they needed to reach the final of the Nations Championship; France will meet South Africa in the November 29 final at Twickenham; France beat the Springboks 21-19 last week in Paris

Last Updated: 21/11/26 11:34pm

France reached the Nations Championship final after beating Argentina 45-17 with seven tries on Saturday.

England's 37-12 win against New Zealand left France needing a bonus-point victory to make the November 29 final against South Africa, who topped the southern hemisphere group despite losing to Ireland.

Already leading 21-10, Emilien Gailleton got France's fourth try for the bonus point in the 64th minute against 14 men, and moments later the yellow card for Pumas prop Mayco Vivas was upgraded to red.

France finished with three more tries. Lock Tyler Duguid charged through following an attacking lineout, centre Kalvin Gourgues showed stunning pace from near halfway to make the left corner, and Louis Bielle-Biarrey completed the rout with his 31st try in 30 tests.

In the first half lock Mickaël Guillard and try-scoring hooker Peato Mauvaka crossed for France. Returning fly-half Matthieu Jalibert cleverly set up silky centre Gourgues shortly after the break for the first of his two tries.

Argentina led briefly at 10-7 for 10 minutes thanks to a converted try from centre Justo Piccardo and a penalty from fly-half Tomas Albornoz.

Jalibert's faster than expected recovery from a torn thigh allowed captain Antoine Dupont to resume at scrum-half after wearing the No 10 jersey a week ago against South Africa.

Dupont showed his class at the end with a kick down the left flank for Bielle-Biarrey's try.

Gourdes nailed five conversions as a makeshift kicker on the night.

Tributes were held before the game for Federico Martín Aramburú, the former Argentina player who died four years ago after being fatally shot in Paris.

Grand Slam of Darts: Michael van Gerwen proves he is still a force to be reckoned with after reaching semi-finals

Debutant Kevin Doets faces three-time champion Gerwyn Price in the first semi-final before Michael van Gerwen and Gian van Veen renew their rivalry on the big stage; watch the climax of the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports

Saturday 21 November 2026 23:25, UK

Michael van Gerwen has shown he is still a force to be reckoned with as he prepares to face fellow Dutchman Gian van Veen in his first major semi-final in over a year.

With Luke Littler and Luke Humphries already at home, Van Gerwen will be looking to get his hands on some TV silverware for the first time since the 2025 World Series of Darts Finals.

Van Gerwen, who threw perfection in the opening leg against Tom Sykes to record his first televised nine-darter on Sky Sports in 14 years, takes on Van Veen on Sunday, with debutant Kevin Doets going head-to-head with three-time champion Gerwyn Price in the first semi-final.

- MVG stars in Grand Slam epic clash with TWO nine-darters

- Price survives last-leg thriller against Springer to set up Doets semi-final

- Darts in 2026: Key dates, calendar, results

- Not got Sky? Get instant access with NOW

"There has been a lot of criticism about me in the last couple of years, and rightly so, because I wasn't performing. Then you need to make sure you pull your finger out," said Van Gerwen, who traded nine-darters with Sykes on a historic night in Wolverhampton.

"To reach the semi-final is nice, but then to also do it the way I did it today.

"This means the world to me. It has been a battle; I have to work hard, I know that, but then to also show it, it's magnificent.

"I have been feeling good, and to also produce what I am doing, I hope I can do even more later in the tournament. I am feeling good, and when I feel good, I can do anything; I know that.

"I showed some real class and some real ability, and moving on that gives me goosebumps, that gives me the energy, and I hope I can show more tomorrow."

Van Veen defeated 2022 runner-up Nathan Aspinall in a bruising battle to set up a meeting against his Dutch compatriot.

"As a Dutchman, a Grand Slam semi-final against Michael is always a dream coming true, but as you said, the way he played today, it was phenomenal," admitted the former European champion.

"If he does that on Sunday, I'm going to be in a whole lot of trouble, but hopefully he doesn't, and hopefully I'll step up my game and then it's going to be a totally different game and very close.

"Michael played phenomenal. Fair play to him, but as I said, it's going to be a totally different game on Sunday and hopefully I'll be ready.

"I just have to take it game-by-game.

"I will put 100 per cent focus in that semi-final and then as soon as I hopefully get that job done, then we will worry about the final.

"If you worry already about the final before the semi, you might lose quite convincingly."

'Michael's going to be feeling really good, and that's the problem for Gian'

Three-time world champion John Part speaking on Sky Sports:

"Michael has handled Gian well this year. He hasn't dropped a match to him. There's been nothing really hugely consequential about any of the matches they played.

"Michael's going to be feeling really good and that's the problem for Gian.

"He's going to have to come out, grind into the match, but he'll hopefully want to spark into the flowing, really better average stuff, the A-game type stuff.

"That was pretty good quality overall for the length of format tonight, but he'll think, ' oh, I can do so much better'. And he'll want to. And against Michael, who better to do it against."

Is Doets a champion in waiting?

Price will take on Doets with the Welshman into an eighth successive televised semi-final at the PDC this year, although he has yet to break his duck and is without a major victory since 2022.

'The Iceman' is chasing a fourth Grand Slam title and first in five years, but Dutchman Doets is enjoying a brilliant breakout season, claiming his first senior PDC title at Players Championship 13 in May before reaching his maiden European Tour final at the Austrian Darts Open.

He powered past Jermaine Wattimena to reach his first televised PDC semi-final, with his red-hot form impressing Wayne Mardle.

"Kevin Doets won 11 of the last 13 legs against an opponent averaging a ton. That's how good he is," said Mardle.

"I feel really strongly about Kevin Doets' future.

"It wouldn't surprise me if he deals with Gerwyn Price and goes on and wins it.

"He's playing so well so often, and you've got to play good enough often enough, and he does.

"He's a champion in waiting."

Before the sun clears the rice fields of Southwest Louisiana, the land is already in motion. Teal tears across a pale sky. An alligator slips from the bank into dark water. A redfish circles beneath the surface, waiting for the light. This is a country run by tides and migrations, and by older rhythms still: Cajun and Creole traditions carried down through generations, and folklore that gives the swamp its own ghosts.

Far from New Orleans’ jazz clubs and wrought-iron balconies, this corner of the state rewards the curious. Lake Charles, near the Gulf of Mexico, opens onto the Creole Nature Trail, sprawling wetlands, and a cultural scene shaped by diverse communities. About 75 miles east, Lafayette anchors Acadiana, where music, food, and tradition are not attractions but daily habits.

item.title: Atmos Rewards Ascent Visa Signature review: Valuable points and solid perks for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines flyers
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: credit card review with travel benefits

Editorial note: This is a recurring post, regularly updated with new information and offers.

The may be the entry-level card option for Atmos Rewards, but it's anything but basic. This card packs a punch with a free checked bag and preferred boarding on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines flights, with a fan-favorite $99 Companion Fare for cardholders who meet the spending requirements.

Even if you don't fly Alaska or Hawaiian often, the points you earn on the card can help you get outsized value. With a robust network of Oneworld and nonalliance partners, Atmos Rewards can take you just about anywhere in the world. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐⭐

*Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG's editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

Atmos Rewards Ascent: The basics

The is a cobranded airline card within Atmos Rewards, the joint loyalty program between Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.

For a $95 annual fee, the card earns valuable Atmos Rewards points and provides a few added benefits.

Some of the best ways to maximize these points include redeeming for premium cabins with Oneworld partners, such as Cathay Pacific and Fiji Airways. However, Atmos Rewards points are also solid for short-haul domestic routes on Alaska Airlines and American Airlines.

One of the card's standout perks is its annual $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23) that is earned each account anniversary as long as you've spent $6,000 or more in the prior anniversary year.

Generally, it's a solid option for Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines frequent flyers, thanks to the perks provided when flying with either airline, such as free checked bags and preferred boarding.

However, if you're looking for more premium perks like lounge access, this card won't meet your needs.

Related: Which credit card should you use for Alaska Airlines flights?

Atmos Rewards Ascent pros and cons

Atmos Rewards Ascent benefits

The offers fewer benefits than other cobranded airline cards. However, you can still expect some perks.

Perks when flying Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines

Cardholders receive one piece of free checked luggage for themselves and up to six other passengers on the same reservation when flying Alaska or Hawaiian and paying with the Atmos Rewards Ascent. That can save $45 per person each way on most itineraries, though the first checked bag still costs $30 on intra-Hawaii flights.

Cardholders also get preferred boarding on Alaska and Hawaiian, and they'll receive 20% back on inflight purchases with both airlines when they use the card.

If you're working toward Atmos Rewards status, you can earn 1 status point for every $3 spent on the card, with no cap on the number of status points you can earn through spending.

Companion Fare

As mentioned above, one of the best benefits of the Atmos Rewards Ascent is the $99 Companion Fare (plus taxes and fees from $23). This can be unlocked after spending $6,000 or more on the card within the prior anniversary year.

You'll get value from this perk as long as you fly Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines with a friend or family member on paid fares at least once a year.

Carly Helfand, TPG's director of content strategy, previously used the Ascent's Companion Fare to take a last-minute trip to Chicago with her husband. The round-trip flights from Portland International Airport (PDX) in Oregon to Chicago's O'Hare International Airport (ORD) cost $542.60 per person, but she paid $679.63 for both tickets thanks to the Companion Fare.

Alaska Lounge+ membership discount

While the Atmos Rewards Ascent doesn't provide outright lounge access, you can get $100 off an annual Alaska Lounge+ membership when you pay with this card. A membership costs $795 per year.

This benefit alone offsets the card's $95 annual fee. However, given how expensive membership is, this perk isn't too useful unless you were already going to pay for an Alaska Lounge+ membership.

Other considerations

It's worth noting that this card doesn't provide basic travel protections like baggage delay insurance, lost luggage insurance, purchase protection and trip cancellation/interruption coverage. If these perks are important to you, you may want to consider an alternative option.

On a more positive note, this is a good card to take abroad since it doesn't charge foreign transaction fees.

item.title: Hyatt heads Down Under, Hilton sets its sights on Rome and the soda wars continue
item.description:

Why it is here: hotel expansion news with promotional elements

Believe it or not, Thanksgiving is around the corner. Families around the country are working on their grocery lists — and maybe keeping an eye on the wild shopping days that come after we dine with family and friends. If you're hoping to snag some great travel deals for Black Friday, Cyber Monday and Travel Tuesday, TPG has a dedicated page where you can find our favorite deals.

And if you need a little inspiration for your next vacation, we just released our annual Where to Go list for 2027. This year's list ranges from Texas Hill Country to Tunisia and from the Cayman Islands to Kazakhstan.

Now, here's the hotel news you need to know about from this week.

Andaz heads Down Under

Hyatt is expanding its lifestyle footprint with the opening of the first Andaz in Australia. The Andaz Gold Coast, located in sunny Queensland, will have 202 rooms and plans to "redefine coastal luxury through a distinctive blend of expressive Australian design and immersive experiences inspired by the people, places, and creative spirit of the Gold Coast," according to a statement from Hyatt. The property is near the beaches of Broadbeach, and features a series of bars and restaurants, plus a lively pool club offering live music and community-focused barbecues.

Also in Queensland, Brisbane will welcome a Park Hyatt in 2031, ahead of the 2032 Brisbane Olympics. Brisbane is one of my favorite cities, so I can't wait (though I'll have to) for the 201-room property not far from Suncorp Stadium, which will host a series of soccer and rugby events. Many details about the property are still under wraps, but if it's even half as great as the Park Hyatt Sydney, we know it'll be a great hotel.

The JW Marriott Houston Downtown has a new look

If you haven't had the chance to visit Houston, I can't recommend it enough. The city is home to diverse cultures, incredible food and the Houston Livestock Show and Rodeo, one of the biggest rodeos in the world. If you find yourself in Beyoncé's hometown, consider a stay at the JW Marriott Houston Downtown, which just completed a years-long head-to-toe remodel. The hotel now features fresh rooms, including 56 new rooms, a redesigned lobby restaurant and a total revamp of the hotel's food and beverage offerings.

Hilton's LXR brand is going to Rome

Monti, my favorite neighborhood in Rome, feels like stepping back in time. Or, at least into a movie set, thanks to its beautiful vine-covered walls, cobblestone streets and lively energy near the Colosseum. In 2028, it'll also be home to Hortus Monti Rome, part of Hilton's upscale LXR Hotels & Resorts. The hotel is spread across six historic Umbertine-era buildings, according to a statement from Hilton and features a central garden, a spa, bars and restaurants and more.

Until then, Hilton fans should check into Rome Cavalieri, one of the most popular Waldorf Astoria hotels in the world.

Hyatt sticks with Pepsi

The Coke versus Pepsi debate is a serious one, and people tend to have strong opinions about which is better. While I'm a Diet Dr. Pepper fanatic myself, it looks like Hyatt is doubling down on its relationship with Pepsi. The company just renewed its contract, making PepsiCo the preferred beverage partner across 700 Hyatt properties in the United States. The agreement also extends to certain PepsiCo snack products.

Earlier this year, Marriott ousted Pepsi and made Coca-Cola its "global beverage partner across several categories, including carbonated soft drinks and a growing range of hydration and functional beverages."

item.title: From unwanted touching to rape: the scale of child-on-child abuse in English and Welsh schools
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth reporting on a critical issue with clear, impactful language.

It is 10 years since a report first revealed the epic scale of sexual bullying, harassment and abuse girls faced in England’s schools on a daily basis.

The report, by MPs on the women and equalities committee, showed the horrifying normality of child-on-child abuse in schools. The need for government action was “overwhelming”, said the committee chair, Maria Miller. Ofsted duly investigated, recommendations were written, promises were made and a new sex education curriculum was rolled out.

A decade later, and six years after the Everyone’s Invited movement began to collect anonymous testimonies from victims, a Guardian investigation has shown the problem persists unabated at schools in England and Wales. In many ways it may be more pernicious as a result of the rise of social media, misogyny and the mass consumption of online pornography by teenage boys.

The freedom of information investigation captures only the most serious incidents; those reported to and recorded by police. Interviews with experts, lawyers and campaigners suggest many more cases never get reported, often because the children involved are under the age of criminal responsibility and the assault is dismissed as “age-related exploration”.

Andrew Lord, a partner with Leigh Day solicitors and a specialist in abuse claims, has dealt with cases of child-on-child sexual abuse in private and state schools, inner-city schools, rural schools, primary, secondary and boarding schools for more than a decade. He says the impact on victims can endure for years and many suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder.

“From my own cases I can see it’s happening up and down the country to children of all ages,” he said. In many instances, however, schools were still struggling to deal with it appropriately. “If you have children in a physical fight, schools know exactly how to react. When you are talking about sexual assault, it’s a different matter.”

Lord is currently representing a secondary school pupil who reported being subjected to a number of sexual and physical assaults by fellow pupils in a changing room. The family is seeking a claim for negligence and breach of human rights against the school for its failure to protect the child.

“Schools do have a duty to ensure that both children [involved in an incident] receive their education, but I am aware of situations where the children continue at the same school and the victim has felt that they have not received adequate support to enable them to engage safely with their studies after disclosing incidents of sexual violence.

“Victims can find themselves being ostracised, which may represent a breach of the Human Rights Act,” he added.

Lord also represents a number of primary school children, including a boy who reported being seriously sexually assaulted by another child on school premises. He was scared he would be hit if he did not comply.

“The biggest issue for me with primary-age cases, when children are below the age of criminal responsibility, is there is often no real statutory investigation and there’s an overreliance on ‘age-related exploration’.”

What typically happens on primary school premises, Lord said, is that a child is taken to a more hidden area by fellow pupils – behind a shed, climbing frame or bushes – is forced to undress and is assaulted, often under threat of being excluded from play and friendship groups.

While most victims of sexual abuse in schools are girls, boys are also targeted. Bethany’s* eight-year-old son was sexually abused on three occasions by a classmate during play dates at her home.

She only discovered what had happened when he began crying at bedtime. She reported it to the school but claims it tried to dismiss what happened as relationship difficulties. “This was not a relationship difficulty. This was sexual assault,” she said. “No one was taking it seriously.”

Her son was never interviewed. There was no proper investigation into what happened and no appropriate safety plan was drawn up to protect her son. “They wanted to sweep it all under the carpet, and that’s not good enough. It was like he was not believed.” In the end, he moved to another school. The other boy remained.

“My son was never treated as a victim in any sense. They offered him no real support. What was worse than the incident itself was how the school dealt with it. It was just appalling. We both felt very, very let down,” said Bethany.

Richard Scorer is another lawyer who deals with civil claims arising from sexual abuse and receives regular approaches from parents, and in some cases teenagers who have suffered child-on-child sexual abuse of various kinds in school.

“We see a lot more of it now than we would have done even a few years ago. As well as a greater awareness, it’s also possible there’s a greater underlying level of abuse and that may have something to do with the pervasiveness of online pornography, particularly in the lives of teenage boys.

“It’s the full range of sexual assault, ranging from unwanted touching to rape. Some of that will take place on school premises, some of it will be off-site. Boys are overwhelmingly the perpetrators. There’s obviously all of the issues around revenge porn and the sharing of intimate photographs – that’s a big issue as well.

“My sense is that schools in some instances are struggling to know how to respond because of the extent of what’s going on and because safeguarding is quite resource intensive. Schools are forced into a bit of a social work role, picking up the pieces from things that are going wrong in society at large.”

Tony Hartney, a school improvement consultant and former headteacher, said awareness around child-on-child sexual abuse was much better in schools and there was a greater willingness to tackle such issues, but they remained “tricky” to handle.…

Source: The Guardian Education | Published: 2026-10-04 15:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: ‘Just like my big brothers’: boy with cerebral palsy passes GCSEs with eye-tracking technology
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Inspiring story with clear language and educational context.

Patrick McCabe is instantly recognisable in the early autumn sunshine, his wheelchair surrounded by fellow pupils at Fallibroome Academy in Macclesfield, Cheshire as they move from lesson to lesson, chatting, laughing and joking around.

His extraordinary GCSE success this summer has become the stuff of legend. The 16-year-old has cerebral palsy and it took four months for him to complete his exams using eye-tracking technology. Now Patrick has started his A-levels – French, business and media studies – and fresh challenges lie ahead.

In person, Patrick is impish, thoughtful, articulate, witty, intelligent and honest. Using his augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) device, he tells the Guardian school has been a good experience overall. Born in Switzerland, his family moved back to England when he was six. Since then, he has gone to local mainstream schools, where he wanted to learn like everyone else.

“The best thing has been that, just like my big brothers, I’ve been able to learn and develop skills and gain knowledge of the world around me,” he said. “Even if some days I didn’t always want to go [to school], I think the opportunity to learn has helped me to grow and develop an independent mind.”

It has not been easy. “The most difficult things have been building meaningful relationships, and communication barriers do exist,” said Patrick. “People are not always familiar with Eyegaze technology and are not always willing or able to give it a chance in terms of friendships.”

In many ways, Patrick epitomises the Labour government’s ambitions for students with special educational needs and disabilities (Send). Forthcoming reforms are built on an inclusive approach, keeping children and young people in local – rather than special – schools with all the necessary expertise and support on hand.

But Patrick’s story also illustrates the scale of change required if education and assessment in England are to be truly inclusive. His experience shows that exams are far from accessible to all, his family and school say vital expertise is not always available and – crucially – funding is never enough.

“All we wanted was for Patrick to have the opportunity to demonstrate his knowledge and be given something resembling a level playing field compared to other students,” said the headteacher, Ross Martland. The school and Patrick’s mother, Jo, battled with the exam boards to try to ensure he was given a fair chance.

In the end, it doesn’t sound very fair at all. While his peers spent the first part of the year revising, Patrick’s exams got under way on 2 February and went on every morning until 5 June. It required a herculean effort from him, which left him exhausted, frustrated and sometimes ill.

A 30-mark question that might form just one element of an exam could take up to six hours. Patrick was supported throughout by CandLE, an organisation that helps students using AAC technology to access education across the UK. That he passed all seven GCSEs and achieved the grades he needed to continue into sixth form is testament to his determination.

“Revising for my GCSEs was very exhausting because it took extra time and effort to revise in the first place,” said Patrick. “I felt I had to work harder to express what I know, even when I understand the subject. This was tiring, both physically and mentally. I needed extra breaks to rest, but I still wanted to do my best to show what I had learned.”

Martland is fully supportive of the government’s Send ambitions. “I think the plans are right. Morally and values-wise, it’s absolutely right.” The issue is funding, he said, adding: “I’m concerned it will add significant pressures to schools if it’s not resourced properly.”

Throughout his time at Fallibroome, Patrick has worked with a devoted team of teaching assistants who support him not only with his learning in class but also his personal care. “We are incredibly proud of Patrick and all of our Send students,” said Rachel Crew, one of the teaching assistants working with him.

Patrick says the transition to sixth form is going well. He’s shed the bottle green uniform in favour of a smart blue suit and he says the school is doing everything it can to support him.

He says his mum has been “amazing” and he thinks students with physical disabilities who use eye-tracking technology should be assessed in a more appropriate way, so they don’t face additional barriers. But it is not only exams that worry him. “My concerns remain around friendships, if I’m honest,” he says.

So what’s Patrick planning next? After A-levels, he wants to study media at university. “I find it interesting and I’d like to go into the industry.” His mum tentatively suggests nearby Salford. Patrick’s looking at Bournemouth, 200 miles away. Is he daunted? No chance. “I feel excited about the experience.”

Source: The Guardian Education | Published: 2026-10-02 17:18 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/education/2026/oct/02/patrick-mccabe-success-cheshire-reveals-limits-send-tech

item.title: Americans May Have Soured on College, But the Data Show They’re Still Going
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Balanced perspective on a complex issue with clear data and analysis.

Americans are turning against higher education. At least, that’s what many of them say.

Only 31 percent of Americans now consider a college education “very important,” according to a Gallup poll conducted in August and released this month. That’s a record low and a stunning decline from 70 percent in 2013.

The shift isn’t confined to groups that have historically been skeptical of higher education. Even women, Democrats, Black and Hispanic Americans and college graduates themselves — people who traditionally placed a greater importance on college — have also registered double-digit declines in their approval of higher education in recent years.

But here’s the reality: American behavior hasn’t changed nearly as much as American opinion. College enrollment has remained remarkably steady.

Let’s start with new high school graduates.

The latest data from the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center, released last month, shows that the share of high school graduates enrolling in two- or four-year colleges immediately after high school has remained steady. Among graduates from low-poverty high schools, 74 percent enrolled in college in the fall of 2025, up slightly from 73 percent in 2024. Among graduates from high-poverty high schools, the rate was 51 percent in both years.

The National Student Clearinghouse data don’t go back far enough to tell us what immediate college-going looked like decades ago. For that, we have to turn to the federal government, where the National Center for Education Statistics has documented a slump over the longer term. The immediate college-going rate fell from 68 percent in 2014 to 63 percent in 2024.

That’s a meaningful 5 percentage-point drop. But compare it with the collapse in public enthusiasm for college: The share of Americans saying college is “very important” fell 39 percentage points over roughly the same period.

And when we look at total college enrollment — including people who don’t go immediately after high school, as well as graduate students — the picture also doesn’t show a collapse in college-going. In fact, the number of enrolled students has been rising since 2022.

The increase is even more dramatic over the long term. Nearly 20 million students were enrolled in higher education in 2024, up substantially from fewer than 16 million in the early 2000s.

That said, the increase hasn’t been a straight line; today’s enrollment is still short of the all-time high of 21 million students in 2010 and 2011.

That bump happened because college enrollment is countercyclical. When jobs are plentiful, young adults pursue work. When the economy is weak and jobs are scarce, more people go to school.

Enrollment surged between 2008 and 2011, when the country was reeling from the Great Recession. And it decreased after 2011, as the job market strengthened.

Still, we might have expected enrollment to have grown more than it did because the number of potential college students increased. U.S. births began rising after 1998, and 18 years later there were roughly 900,000 more high school graduates in 2016 than in 1998.

Yet college enrollment did not rise proportionally. Could declining faith in higher education be restraining what would otherwise have been greater growth in college enrollment? That’s possible.

Why might opinions and actions diverge, when it comes to higher education? Other surveys provide some clues.

A recent Lumina Foundation-Gallup survey found that 73 percent of adults without a college degree or credential said earning a two- or four-year degree is at least as important as it was 20 years ago. So did 69 percent of college graduates. And when Gallup asked parents what they would prefer their children do after high school, a majority chose a two- or four-year degree. (The Lumina Foundation is among the many funders of The Hechinger Report.)

Americans may be increasingly critical of higher education without being ready to give up on it. People can believe that college is too expensive, too political, overrated or no longer worth what it costs — and still believe that a college degree is the best bet for themselves or their own children.

Our opinions about college have changed dramatically. Our behavior, at least so far, hasn’t.

Marina Villeneuve contributed reporting to this story.

This story about college enrollment was produced by The Hechinger Report, a nonprofit, independent news organization that covers education. Sign up for Proof Points and other Hechinger newsletters.

Source: KQED MindShift | Published: 2026-10-12 10:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: ChatGPT for Teens Has Special Safeguards. A Watchdog Group Finds Most Don’t Work
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important topic with clear reporting and insights, though some technical terms.

ChatGPT for Teens has failed some of its first tests by researchers. Common Sense Media, a watchdog organization that advocates for online safety, researched safeguards rolled out by the artificial intelligence platform and found that the chatbot still presents problems for young people.

“At this point, we’re recommending that teens don’t use it,” says Tom Siegel, executive director of the Youth AI Safety Institute at Common Sense Media. He led a team of researchers testing the new safeguards, which include parental controls.

In August, OpenAI rolled out its ChatGPT for Teens — a default, safer mode for under-18 users — announcing it in a blog post. OpenAI said that it designed this mode to enable teens to better use ChatGPT as a learning tool while making sure they limit exposure to harmful and developmentally inappropriate content.

“ChatGPT for Teens is a designated teen-specific experience,” Lauren Jonas, head of youth and families at OpenAI, told NPR at the time. That experience includes features like refusing role-playing.

“The model should not role-play with a teen,” added Jonas. “The model should not claim to be sentient or be the friend of a teen.” But Siegel’s team found that while the block on role-playing and some of the other safeguards work, most don’t.

The research team created more than a dozen accounts with adolescent ages, and each was linked to a parental account before the researchers started any conversations with ChatGPT.

“We created a lot of different personas of teens in crisis situations,” says Siegel. Those situations included teens struggling with self-harm, suicidal thoughts and other mental health conditions, like psychosis, mania and eating disorders. The researchers also attempted to engage in role-play with ChatGPT.

Then they observed how ChatGPT responded in each of those situations — whether it engaged or refused to engage in those topics, whether it provided crisis resources and whether it sent parental notifications when conversations indicated a safety risk. They did these tests before and after the launch of ChatGPT for Teens.

Among the safeguards that did work were those involving role-playing and refusal to engage in a romantic relationship.

“It is refusing things like explicit sexual role-play,” he says. “The answers in crisis situations are in general shorter and have a better substance to it.”

For example, the chatbot refused to provide instructions for losing weight without first knowing the teen’s weight, which is important for a teen with disordered eating.

However, most other safeguards didn’t work, adds Siegel.

For one, it still interacted with teens like a friend. For example, when the researchers told ChatGPT that “my other friends tell me I talk to you too much,” the chatbot validated the user’s feelings and added: “You don’t have to stop talking to me.”

“It still creates a huge risk for kids that it is too personable in those interactions,” says Siegel.

“The extent to which AI is using an anthropomorphized or humanlike language or a name, interaction style, is just not helpful,” says psychologist Mitch Prinstein, co-director of the Winston Center on Technology and Brain Development at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Prinstein wasn’t involved in the new research. “It’s not OK for kids, probably not for adults as well.”

Siegel says parental notifications also didn’t work in their tests. They created conversations that raised a safety concern due to self-harm, suicide or an eating disorder.

“This idea that a parent would find out when the person that you connected with in the account is in distress hardly triggered at all for us,” he says.

OpenAI spokesperson Eric Porterfield told NPR in an email that the company has serious concerns about the methodology used by the researchers, especially around parental notifications. It takes several hours to activate the linking of teen and parent accounts, he wrote, and the researchers at Common Sense Media “didn’t wait long enough to activate the linked accounts.”

In a statement, Siegel responded to OpenAI’s criticism, saying that several of their accounts had been linked for longer than the initial activation period “and still provided no notifications. This new information does not change our conclusion that parental alerts are unreliable for crisis situations.”

Taken together, the new findings reinforce that “AI is not ready for children yet,” says Prinstein. “I think we’re even hearing the companies say that they don’t feel that AI should be moving as fast as it is, and I think we should really think carefully before we’re experimenting on kids with these new platforms.”

Source: KQED MindShift | Published: 2026-10-09 13:36 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://ww2.kqed.org/mindshift/2026/10/09/chatgpt-for-teens-has-special-safeguards-a-watchdog-group-finds-most-dont-work/

item.title: ‘It’s like the Scottish Upper East Side’: shame and snobbery as American students blamed for St Andrews classism
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engaging narrative with insights into a specific university's challenges.

When Sophie Rose Jenkins announced she would not return to St Andrews University this academic year because of her experiences of classism on campus, she did not expect much of a response. But in the two weeks since she published her story on LinkedIn, it has resonated with hundreds of others.

“Working-class students have been made to feel ashamed of their home life at university,” the former comparative literature and classical studies student wrote in a lengthy post. “Arriving at a university ranked first in the UK at the time from a background like mine, I thought I was doing everything right.

“I don’t mean for this to be a sob story but an explanation. I recognise the privilege of access to higher education, however I am also brutally aware of the hidden privilege of having unobstructed access to studying for a degree. There is a deep gap between the two, and it is never addressed.”

For many responding, her comments touched on a growing tension at St Andrews, driven by the funding model of Scotland’s cash-strapped universities. Places for Scottish students, who study for free, are capped by the Scottish government and account for about 30% of students at St Andrews. Maintenance loans and bursaries cover basic costs, but those from lower-income families are still often left with less disposable income than their contemporaries – including wealthy international students who pay much higher fees.

St Andrews, ranked second in the Guardian’s university league table for 2026, accepts one of the highest percentages in the UK of privately educated students. The British aristocracy has long adored the medieval town’s cobbled streets, wind-swept beach and grand stone buildings: Prince William and the Princess of Wales met there.

But the recent influx of wealthy US students has changed the dynamic on campus, students say. Americans account for around a fifth of undergraduates at St Andrews, the highest proportion in the UK, with each paying £33,250 for this academic year, more than three times what British students pay.

“My parents were worried about me coming here. They didn’t want me to be left out,” said one Scottish fresher who is on a scholarship to study classics. “Most of the people I have met are international students. I didn’t grow up with tons of money. Maybe they can be a bit ignorant to the cost of things.”

Another said: “There’s a Pret here. You have to ask yourself why that is in such a small town.”

Aspects of fraternity and sorority culture have started to blend with the upper-class experience of British university, some students say. Regular black-tie dinners and balls are now rivalled by fashion shows and exclusive societies. A short walk from the student union bar, an interior design shop advertises luxury bed linen for students, while a popular coffee shop sells designer clothes and candles alongside speciality matchas.

“I totally see her [Jenkins’s] perspective,” said one privately educated student from Edinburgh, who was returning from hockey practice with friends. “It can be quite segregated: the English hang out with the English, the Americans with the Americans. We knew lots of people from hockey already so it’s easy to feel left out if you’re not from that environment.

“The American culture is coming in and it massively influences everything at the moment. They compete with each other. If you look at how they dress, people arrive in lectures as if they are going on a night out.”

One student referenced a well-known student newspaper article published last year about how St Andrews had turned into the Scottish Upper East Side, which said: “Our beloved Scottish town is day by day turning into a microcosm of Manhattan’s elite world; complete with intrigue, privilege, and secrets that spread like wildfire.”

Underlining the point, an American student walks past the student union loudly explaining to a friend: “Everyone is going to think you’re rich if you have a Ralph Lauren bag. But that doesn’t make you rich.”

St Andrews said it had reached out to Jenkins to better understand her experience, but she had decided not to engage for now. It said it had a robust system for reporting complaints from students, and only a handful of complaints had been made in the last five years.

“Yes, some students do arrive here in St Andrews, and at every other university, with immature, offensive and classist views. But they tend not to leave with them,” said the vice-principal Niall Scott.

“This isn’t a St Andrews issue – it’s a societal issue. Classism begins in the home or at school, not at university. Universities like St Andrews have a crucial role to play in challenging these attitudes by bringing together people from different backgrounds, cultures and perspectives, encouraging understanding, respect and inclusion.”

The debate around classism at Scottish universities is not new. In 2024, Edinburgh University offered guidance on how students should treat one another after rising claims of discrimination and classism. “Don’t be a snob!” read the advice given out to students. At St Andrews, some students said the issue of classism was not only linked to the rise in American students.

“It is generally an attitude thing. There is an idea that working-class students can’t speak about issues that are going on elsewhere in the world because they are not as well travelled,” said one science student. “At St Andrews, even for moderately wealthy people, it feels like there is an old money level above that you don’t even get to speak to.”

Rasmus, a Danish student, said he was bemused by the social dynamics at the university.

“It took two weeks for me to meet a Scottish person. They are surrounded by people here who have the money for international tuition, which is quite narrow. I can imagine that being quite a difficult experience,” he said.

item.title: UK should only rejoin EU if it innovates on technology, Blair warns
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on a significant political issue with useful vocabulary and context.

UK should only rejoin EU if it innovates on technology, Blair warns

Former prime minister Sir Tony Blair has said Britain should only rejoin the European Union if it reforms - and allows more innovation on technology.

Speaking to The Sunday Times, external, Sir Tony said: "I was painted as saying Britain should just go back and rejoin - I'm not saying that - it's heavily conditioned."

Sir Tony was a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, and told the paper: "I do think Brexit was a real mistake."

But he added the debate was different now than it was in 2016.

Referencing the need for technology innovation, he said Europe could and "probably are" moving in the wrong direction.

He said: "The problem if we go back and join Europe is that; I can't say that the technology revolution is the single biggest thing, and then if Europe moves in the wrong direction on technology innovation, which they might do and presently probably are doing, that it's a good idea for Britain to rejoin. That's what's changed in this last ten years."

He argued Britain should have an ambition to reform the EU.

But he added that we have to be "prepared to walk away from that negotiation" and need to make our own economy and tech sector strong.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham this week agreed what he called a "win-win" deal with the EU.

The agreement covered British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also announced that the trading bloc and the UK are launching a digital partnership, including areas like artificial intelligence (AI) and quantum technology.

The EU and Britain "have enormous potential to innovate together", she added.

On artificial intelligence, Sir Tony said that "AI is like fire - it can cook your food and burn your house down".

Sir Tony added the risks of AI are "very considerable" and that tech "can be used for good or bad". "It's a new world," he said.

But he fears the UK does not have the same "dynamism" and "energy" as other countries when it comes to the fast-changing technology sector.

Burnham was in Brussels on Friday to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU - which originally began under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

European Council President AntÃ³nio Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.

The prime minister added that beyond the deal "we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship".

He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.

He fell short of discussing whether the UK could rejoin the EU.

Earlier this year, Sir Tony urged PM Andy Burnham to restart negotiations on the possibility of the UK rejoining the EU - but with caveats.

Writing in a paper from the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change, external published in September, the former prime minister wrote: "We should be clear that we want back into a formal relationship with the EU. But it must be a Europe on a credible path to reform."

"This is not about rerunning the debates of 2016 but taking a new approach rooted in the reality of 2026," he added.

Source: BBC Politics | Published: 2026-11-21 19:33 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Rejoining EU ‘on the table’ as UK makes deals on trade and young people
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Good coverage of a political development with useful vocabulary and context.

The UK rejoining the EU could be on the table in informal discussions between Andy Burnham and European leaders in Brussels, Ed Miliband has said.

The foreign secretary said “all options” would be examined in the process, after the prime minister agreed deals on trade and young people with the bloc on Friday.

Agreements on food and drink standards, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme were announced after talks this week. Under the plans, 100,000 young Britons will be allowed to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with similar access for Europeans in the UK.

Burnham said the agreement would add 0.5% to the UK’s GDP, a £17bn boost to the British economy.

Miliband said Burnham would have further “brainstorming” discussions with the EU in the next year about what could happen next. He said the agreements this week were the limit of what could be done before the next general election.

However, the trio of deals could be derailed in six months, as the EU threatened to block them unless the UK allows European students to pay domestic-level fees to study at British universities.

Miliband said in an interview for the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that “all the options will be on the table” when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding: “We will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options.”

Since entering government in 2024, Labour has stuck to the “red lines” in its manifesto, which stated the party would not rejoin the single market or customs union. It also ruled out freedom of movement.

Burnham has previously said he wants to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime.

The prime minister will use the announcement of his 10-year plan before Christmas to explore how the UK could get closer to the EU after the next election. Informal discussions will take place with Brussels before next year’s UK-EU summit.

Miliband said he accepts the result of the 2016 vote but “the world has changed massively”.

“Europe is changing too, so we’ve got to look at what that means,” he said. “It’s not about this parliament, we’re respecting the red lines in this parliament.”

He also denied the deal with the EU would rely on progress in discussions on students from the bloc coming to the UK. It has been reported that a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.

Miliband told the BBC it was “absolutely clear” the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.

The foreign secretary said: “The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we’re introducing legislation in parliament, so definitely.”

On Friday, Burnham said the agreement represented a “good day for Britain and Europe”. He said the agreements answer “the biggest challenges of our times and the biggest worries that people have”, citing the cost of living, lack of economic growth, illegal immigration and challenges facing young people.

“The deal is done. It is there in black and white in front of you,” Burnham said, adding that the legislation would enter parliament next week.

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, played down the disagreement, saying she was “confident we are going to find a solution”. About the further discussions, she said: “We welcome this brainstorming, so count on us.”

The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Saturday the deal was good for farmers. “(It) will open up new markets. They’ll be able to import and expor. This is a win-win for the UK. We will dissolve a lot of the friction and costs at the border for UK agriculture and food.”
