item.title: An effort to circumvent the Electoral College may be within reach. But hurdles remain
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed reporting on a political effort with useful vocabulary and context.

An effort to circumvent the Electoral College may be within reach. But hurdles remain

A national effort to ensure that only winners of the popular vote become president could reach a critical milestone soon.

It's a possible outcome of huge Democratic wins in this month's midterm elections.

Next year, Democrats will fully control five states that could sign the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their presidential electoral votes to the winner of the nationwide popular vote, not the winner of their respective states.

If they do join other 18 Democratic-led states — plus the District of Columbia — that are in the compact, the effort will have surpassed the needed 270 electoral votes required to go into effect, making an end run around the Electoral College. So far no Republican-led states have joined the compact and the party is largely not unified on the issue.

There are still plenty of political, practical and legal hurdles that this effort would need to clear. But proponents are optimistic many of those hurdles will be cleared – even perhaps in time for the next presidential election.

"I've never been more confident that 63% of American voters can get what they want in the 2028 presidential election, which is a national popular vote for president." Patrick Rosenstiel, a senior consultant to National Popular Vote, the group pushing for the compact in states across the country, told NPR, referencing Pew polling.

Right now, the compact has a total of 222 electoral votes. The five states that will soon be completely in the hands of Democrats – Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Nevada and Wisconsin – add up to 61 electoral votes. Combinations of at least four of those states would put the compact over 270.

So far, governors and incoming governors in Pennsylvania and Nevada have said they are open to signing legislation that would bring their states into the interstate agreement. But other governors have yet to publicly weigh in.

One of the looming questions over these efforts is whether these states – all presidential battlegrounds – would be willing to give up their immense influence in elections ahead of the 2028 presidential contests.

And leaders in each state will also have to weigh whether they want to be the tipping point in moving forward a movement that could upend how the U.S. decides presidential winners.

Already, some Democrats are more reticent on the issue than they were before. For example, Democratic Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs, who had previously supported the measure, has not commented recently on whether the state's new Democratic majorities should sign on. NPR reached out to Hobbs' office for comment but did not receive a response before publication.

And then of course, there are the various legal and logistical hurdles.

The practical and legal hurdles

Some legal scholars have observed that this agreement between states could run afoul of the compact clause in the Constitution, which says that "no state shall, without the consent of Congress … enter into any agreement or compact with another state … unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay."

Norman Miller, a constitutional law professor at Willamette University, said that beyond the legal hurdles, he sees a range of practical issues with the compact.

Mostly, he said, it could upend what is a core feature of American presidential elections, which is that they are largely decentralized.

States individually decide who can vote and how they can vote. He said forcing electors from one state to vote according to the tallies in another state could create some tension.

"We would want to have a standardized, uniform set of rules regarding who gets to vote for president, how they vote, how those votes are tabulated, and to have a federal election authority doing that tabulation," he said. "I think trying to nationalize [the current system] and entrusting a national election to 51 separate election administrators would just sow discord and distrust."

But John Koza, the chairman of National Popular Vote, said if the compact works the way it is supposed to, none of that will be necessary.

"We don't need a centralized bureaucracy or a presidentially appointed commission that could be manipulated," he told NPR. "The simple fact is current state and federal law provide for the issuance of a certified vote count from each state. And all that has to be done is add them up."

But mostly, Miller said the biggest question before this effort is whether such a large reform should be done via a constitutional amendment.

Upending the Electoral College, some argue, would be a profound change to how the U.S. chooses the leader of the free world. Opponents of a national popular vote, such as Save Our States, argue that without the incentives created by the Electoral College, American politics will move more toward "toward more regional politics and would exacerbate existing divides."

Miller said even though it will be much more difficult to pull off, it would be worth going through a more fulsome process via Article 5 to get rid of the Electoral College, instead of working around it.

"This is where I think process matters," he said. "If you really want to have a national popular vote for the president and avoid all of the legal and practical difficulties, you need to do that through a constitutional amendment, because only a constitutional amendment can address the legal and practical challenges of conducting a national popular vote for the presidency."

A similar effort to pass an amendment to get rid of the Electoral College in 1969 failed, though. And very few amendments have even gotten close to passing in recent history.

Rosenstiel, the consultant to the National Popular Vote, said this is why he thinks groups like his are seeking a creative solution to something most Americans agree is a problem.…

Source: NPR Politics | Published: 2026-11-21 10:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.npr.org/2026/11/21/nx-s1-6044237/electoral-college-national-popular-vote-interstate-compact

item.title: South Korea’s Coal Use Is Surging – and Not Just Because of the Iran War
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important topic with useful vocabulary and context, though not as in-depth as others.

A year ago this week at COP30, climate advocates and high ambition states celebrated South Korea for joining the Powering Past Coal Alliance. But in the course of the past year, coal has become South Korea’s largest power source, at 30 percent from January to July, ahead of nuclear, which led last year. Australia saw thermal coal shipments to South Korea more than triple year-on-year in the June quarter, even while Canberra served as president of negotiations at this year’s climate talks in Turkiye.

Last year, South Korea pledged to close 40 of its 61 coal units by 2040. However, in March, Seoul loosened a key cap that limited coal plant output to reduce fine dust emissions, allowing plants to run at up to 100 percent on low fine-dust days. Now, with colder winter weather and rising energy demand, air pollution from coal generation is likely to rise, according to a spokesperson for South Korea’s Ministry of Climate, Energy, and Environment.

ost accounts blamed Seoul’s turn back toward coal on the war with Iran and related shocks to the energy system. But data suggests South Korea’s current transition pains began before the war in the Gulf. In the first quarter of 2026, South Korea’s nuclear power generation fell 23 percent. Then, after Israel and the United States began their strikes on Iran on February 28, gas prices spiked. With both nuclear and gas generation compromised, Seoul surged coal imports and generation to fill the gap.

In the first half of 2026, nuclear generation was 82.08 TWh, down 17.0 percent from 98.87 TWh, according to KEPCO’s monthly statistics. Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power, a state-owned utilities company, blamed it on overlapping planned maintenance. According to KHNP, the combined maintenance days across the fleet jumped from 404 to 1,048 days.

The Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air said that older reactors went offline as their 40-year operating licenses expired, causing additional disruption and compounding the shortfall left by maintenance. The nuclear reactors named Hanbit 1 and 2 have remained idle awaiting licensing decisions, according to the World Nuclear Association. Kori 4, a nuclear reactor near Busan, shut down in August 2025, and only last month did the regulator clear Kori 4, extending its life to 2035.

Gas is often thought of as a support or backup for the renewable energy transition because, unlike nuclear, it can quickly be turned off and on. But in 2026, global LNG supply buckled, hitting Asian and Pacific economies particularly hard. For South Korea, LNG generation fell around 6 percent, according to Ember, a global energy think tank.

“This winter shows that heavy dependence on imported fossil fuels, whether LNG or coal, is itself an energy security problem,” said Yun Sun-jin, dean of the Graduate School of Environmental Studies at Seoul National University.

“LNG is not only a fossil fuel, it also leaves Korea exposed to price shocks and supply disruptions. If gas is meant to be the bridge, the bridge itself is unstable,” she said.

From January to July 2026 South Korea’s coal generation rose 18 percent, shoring up the losses in the energy supply. And some are worried about what that might mean for air pollution, not to mention emissions contributing to climate change.

Asked what criteria determine which days coal output can be increased without worsening fine dust, a climate ministry spokesperson told The Diplomat, “An increase in coal-fired power generation would also lead to higher levels of fine particulate matter and there is no particular standard to apply.”

“The government needs clear, public criteria for when coal plants are ramped up, so that health protections during high-concentration periods are not eroded,” said Yun.

South Korea has struggled to manage air pollution, particularly in provinces like South Chungcheong. According to a 2023 study by CREA and Solutions for Our Climate, coal plant pollution caused almost 2,000 premature deaths in two years. No estimate has been published for 2026, but the ministry itself admitted that more coal use means more fine dust.

The role of coal in South Korea’s energy system is under a great deal of scrutiny. Hadong 1 and Boryung 5, two coal units, were due to close by the end of June, but in April, the closure for both was pushed back to March 2027. Taean 2, another coal plant, was scheduled to close this year too; however, it has been the subject of pressure from local officials and a popular residents’ petition asking for a delay in the closure. No decision has been announced, and climate groups are saying an extension would go against Seoul’s coal phase-out plan. But they are not the only ones worried.

“A temporary increase in coal generation may be justified if LNG supplies are constrained or prices become exceptionally high, but only if the economic benefits outweigh the environmental and health costs,” said Yoo Jong-hyun, an associate professor at Seoul National University’s Graduate School of Public Administration.

“Higher LNG prices alone should not justify abandoning these [environmental] measures,” said Yoo.

Australia, which is currently leading climate negotiations at COP31 in Turkiye, has stood to gain from the surge in coal demand. According to statistics from the Office of the Chief Economist, thermal coal exports to Korea jumped by 241 percent year on year in the June quarter. Since 2022, Australia has approved over ten new coal mines or extensions. Chris Bowen, the minister for climate change and president of negotiations at COP31, did not respond to questions as of press time.

South Korea’s eighth fine-dust management program begins on December 1. It’s unclear how long coal plants will be allowed to keep running at full output on low fine-dust days. A spokesperson for South Korea’s climate ministry said it “remains to be seen” and “will vary depending on domestic and international energy supply and price conditions at that time.”

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-19 20:49 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: China Ratchets Up Its Weaponization of Trade
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important topic with useful vocabulary and context, though not as in-depth as others.

For years, the United States has been using export controls to limit China’s access to advanced technologies. China has repeatedly denounced these measures as “blatant” attempts by the U.S. to strengthen its own “technological hegemony,” arguing that the entire strategy runs “contrary to the principles of market economy.” At the same time, however, China has been steadily building its capacity to retaliate.

China has long used punitive trade measures as a political weapon. But in recent years, it has been laying the groundwork for more comprehensive economic statecraft, largely in response to U.S. pressure. In 2019, for example, China created its Unreliable Entities List as a direct response to Huawei’s placement on Washington’s Entity List.

The following year, China passed its Export Control Law, which consolidated a fragmented export-control regime in a single framework. In 2021, China issued “blocking rules,” aimed at shielding Chinese entities from extraterritorial application of foreign laws and sanctions. China has also strengthened its ability to wage trade wars, expanded its dual-use export controls, and created a unified licensing system, which requires transaction-specific approvals, detailed technical disclosures, and end-user verification.

Over the last year, however, China has taken this effort to a new level. Two regulations announced by the State Council in April institutionalized a shift from ad hoc measures to a comprehensive legal framework for countering sanctions, foreign interference, and “long-arm jurisdiction.” Decree 834 established a regime for protecting industrial and supply-chain security, and Decree 835 created a statutory basis for responding to “improper extraterritorial jurisdiction of foreign states.”

Now, the Ministry of Commerce has widened the Chinese export-control regime’s scope beyond military and dual-use domains. The new controls, announced last month, cover AI, tunnel-boring and excavation machinery, specialized maritime and dredging equipment, photovoltaic manufacturing technologies, advanced drones and navigation systems, and biotechnology, including cell and gene therapies and genetic-modification processes. Virtually any industrial capability that gives China a competitive advantage is being recast as a national-security asset and subjected to export curbs.

This expansive export-control system is in key respects modeled on that of the United States. Just as the U.S. uses its huge market and technological leadership for geopolitical ends, China is leveraging its dominance in critical minerals, industrial inputs, and specialized capital goods. But there is an important difference: China’s unique position in the global economy enables it to exploit other countries’ vulnerabilities in ways that the U.S. cannot.

China’s near-monopoly on rare-earth processing and refining, along with its dominance in other critical minerals, is a case in point: it gives the country powerful leverage over a wide range of vital high-tech industries, including electric vehicles (EVs), wind turbines, advanced electronics, and defense manufacturing. China’s control over specialized industrial machinery and its broader centrality to global supply chains offer further sources of leverage.

These amount to potent weapons in China’s geoeconomic arsenal. In April 2025, China halted most exports of rare-earth minerals to the United States, forcing Donald Trump’s administration to reverse its tariff escalation, negotiate a trade truce, and generally shift from confrontation to accommodation.

But China is not reserving these weapons for the U.S. China has restricted exports of critical minerals, manufacturing equipment, tunnel-boring machines, industrial components, battery technologies, and lithium-ion-related inputs to India – a clear bid to impede India’s emergence as an alternative global manufacturing hub.

Similarly, China has imposed export restrictions on Japan, often targeting Japanese companies with ties to the defense industry, in order to exert economic pressure and undermine Japan’s effort to strengthen its military. China can use this leverage against other major economies as well, including the European Union, disrupting EV production, renewable energy projects, defense manufacturing, and major infrastructure investments.

In the long run, China’s export-control regime could prove counterproductive, as it accelerates the global scramble to reduce dependence on its industrial ecosystem. Governments will intensify efforts to diversify mineral supplies, build domestic processing capacity, subsidize strategic industries, and shift manufacturing to more trustworthy countries.

But, by that point, considerable damage may have been done. Already, the normalization of economic coercion by both China and the United States is threatening to splinter a trading system built on interdependence, with fragile global supply chains becoming the first casualty. The result could be a global economy that is divided into competing technological and industrial ecosystems.

This would impose a heavy burden on multinational companies, which would have to navigate two regulatory systems. A firm that depends on U.S. technology but operates in China could be caught between conflicting licensing requirements, sanctions obligations, and end-user restrictions. To satisfy both the U.S. and China, manufacturers might need separate supply chains, technology platforms, and compliance systems. The efficiencies that once made globalization attractive would be sharply eroded.

Middle powers and developing economies are in a particularly uncomfortable position. Not only are they vulnerable to economic coercion by the U.S. and China;…

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-19 18:34 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: ‘It’s Impossible to Refuse’: State-Imposed Forced Labor and Exploitation in Uzbekistan’s Silk Sector
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important topic with useful vocabulary and context, though not as in-depth as others.

Uzbekistan has a favorable climate for silk production, a long tradition of silk making, and rural communities where jobs are scarce. The government sees the industry as a way to create jobs, reduce poverty, and increase export earnings.

What do those ambitions mean for the farmers and rural families who produce silkworm cocoons? A new report by Uzbek Forum for Human Rights documents how farmers are forced to produce cocoons and how rural families who raise silkworms at home face exploitative conditions and struggle to get paid.

A cotton and grain farmer in the arid Kamashi district of Kashkadarya had no mulberry trees with leaves suitable for feeding silkworms. Yet when an Uzbek Forum monitor interviewed him in April 2026, he had already been told to deliver 80 kilograms of cocoons to the district silk processing enterprise.

His land lease required him to grow cotton and grain, there was no obligation to cultivate cocoons.

At the start of the year, the farmer said he signed a blank contract which contained only the stipulated amount of cocoons he was expected to deliver. It was the same procedure as in previous years. He received no copy of the contract and did not know what price he would be paid.

“Maybe they won’t pay me at all,” he said.

The previous year he received no payment because he had fallen short of the quota set by local officials. What he earned from the cocoons he delivered was less than what it cost to produce them because he had to cover the cost of the silkworm eggs and other resources.

All farmers interviewed for the report said they saw little point in producing cocoons but were afraid to refuse.

“It’s easier to agree and buy the cocoons when it’s time to deliver them than to get into a dispute with the district authorities,” was a common explanation.

Uzbekistan has produced silk for centuries and is the world’s third-largest producer of silkworm cocoons, after China and India. The government sees silk products as a strategic export and a source of foreign currency. It also expects the industry to create jobs and reduce poverty in rural areas, where steady work is often hard to find.

The report examines what those ambitions mean for the people who produce the cocoons. Between 2024 and 2026, independent rights monitors conducted 85 interviews with farmers and home-based cocoon producers in 21 districts across five regions of Uzbekistan and Karakalpakstan, reviewed legislation, contracts, media and social media, as well as official documents governing the sector.

The report’s main finding is that the current cocoon production system relies on the state-imposed forced labor of farmers and exploitation of low-income rural families. As a result, there is a substantial gap between the goals of developing the sector and improving rural livelihoods, and the actual conditions faced by cocoon producers.

The Uzbek government retains control over much of the silk industry. It allocates land for mulberry trees (the food base for silkworms), sets production targets, and approves the prices silk enterprises pay for cocoons. As of October 2026, Uzbekistan had 62 silk-processing enterprises, also known as clusters. These are privately owned but operate within government programs to develop the industry.

Each year, the government sets a national cocoon production target. Official decisions describe these figures as “prognoses.” In practice, they are divided among regions and districts and then assigned to individual producers as quotas. Official documents show that cocoons are produced in 150 of the country’s 162 districts and that farmers are assigned about 65 percent of the annual national target.

District governors, known as “hokims,” are assessed on whether their districts meet their targets. This creates an incentive to force cotton and grain farmers to deliver cocoons, even though their land leases do not require it. This use of production targets has deep roots in Uzbek agriculture, particularly in cotton and wheat. In silk cocoon production, it places a separate obligation on farmers who already have crops to tend.

Farmers in Uzbekistan lease their land from the state and depend heavily on local officials for access to land, irrigation water, credit, and machinery. This makes farmers vulnerable to coercion, as challenging the authorities can have serious consequences. Most said they did not even try to object for fear of reprisals.

“They say it’s voluntary, but when the time comes, the prosecutor calls us, the police come to our homes, and the hokim shouts at us and insults us in closed meetings, demanding that we deliver those damned cocoons,” a farmer in the Fergana region said. The arbitrary abuse of power by local officials has also resulted in the use of violence.

In one case in 2025 when a farmer in Kamashi district in Kashkadarya region refused to fulfill his quota, he was handcuffed and beaten by police officers.

The quota is based on how much land a farmer leases and in some cases the quota can be negotiated down with officials. For most, however, cocoon production still means more work and more expense, with little to show for either.

Raising silkworms takes about four weeks and begins in the spring, when cotton and grain farmers are already at their busiest in the fields. Silkworms eat only mulberry leaves, which have to be cut and carried by hand. The larvae need feeding five or six times a day and night. Just a single box of eggs, which yields about 60 kilograms of cocoons, can keep an entire family busy.

Farmers who cannot raise silkworms themselves have to find someone willing to do the work for additional payment or buy cocoons to make up any shortfall in their quotas. They then deliver the cocoons to the district’s silk cluster. The quota system effectively gives private silk enterprises a steady supply of cheap silk cocoons while farmers bear the cost of growing them.…

item.title: The Australian fashion artisans who still make clothes by hand
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, concrete detail

In a world where garment makers are forced to wear AI-training headgear and T-shirts can be ordered from Kmart on Uber Eats, it may seem as if the days of procuring something made by hand from an artisan are numbered.

While jobs in Australian textile, clothing and footwear manufacturing have been in freefall since their 1989 peak – from 115,000 to approximately 30,000 in 2026 – the work of a dressmaker or shoemaker who stitches every piece by hand is even harder to find.

But in certain studios and fitting rooms around the country, tape measures are wielded, fabric is pinched and pinned and the warmth of service extends well beyond holding out an Eftpos machine.

For hand-makers, the work is about more than just another product or a paycheck. The beauty of their vocation is in many small acts: mastering technique, appreciating texture, building a community of clients, and drawing on the mysterious well of creative intuition that allows humans to make wonderful things.

Andrew McDonald has been making shoes for 30 years. But no matter how many times he’s measured a client’s foot, produced a wooden last, selected materials, and cut and stitched the leather, he still worries about the end product.

“We’re always trying to solve problems for the client along the way,” he says. “I’m always thinking, is this good enough?”

The veteran shoemaker studied at Sydney Tafe before leaving to apprentice under Paul Harnden near Aberdeen in Scotland and with the legacy boot manufacturer John Lobb in London. Now, he works out of the Strand Arcade in Sydney’s CBD, employs an apprentice and runs a work experience program.

He produces a range of ready-to-wear leather shoes, alongside a bespoke service that involves a 30-minute consultation and a 16-week manufacturing period that includes three to four fittings. The ready-to-wear shoes cost between $1,000 and $1,200, while custom-made pairs start at $3,600 and range up to $5,000 (returning customers receive a discount of $1,000 to $1,200 to reflect the repeated parts of the process).

Given the cost and the lead time, he’s aware that what he does “is not for everybody”. McDonald is catering to a specific type of person, who is looking to buy into more than just a glossy brand.

“The thing about handmade is, it’s very personalised and at the centre … is the relationship you have with the maker,” he says. “Over the years, we get to see that person a lot, and we get to know who they are.”

Repairability and product longevity are at the heart of this. Although he has many clients who have worn his shoes for years, recently a customer asked to have a pair from the 1990s repaired. McDonald felt it was time to let them go, but the customer had a sentimental attachment and insisted. “I mean, he’s a nut,” says McDonald. “But it goes to show, my business is essentially a relationship business.”

Jeorge Bradford, Iti

Jeorge Bradford makes every single garment for his label, Iti, by himself. Working out of a converted three-car garage on his mother-in-law’s property in Moss Vale in the southern highlands of Australia, he produces a small range of made-to-order shirts and pants defined by panels of latticed fabric.

Bradford, who graduated from the University of Technology Sydney with a bachelor of fashion design and textiles in 2023, developed the weaving technique for a university assignment. “I just really fell in love with it,” he says. He kept wearing the shirts he’d made after graduation, but hadn’t considered launching a brand until someone asked if they could buy one. He now has two stockists and a cult following.

While it varies for each piece, he estimates it takes 48 hours to make the simplest shirt – with prices starting at $250. Generally, the time between an order being placed and delivery is two to three weeks. While the process is so time intensive, or until he hires some staff, it will be difficult for Iti to scale, but for Bradford, fast growth is not really the point. “Whether it’s uber-successful or not, I’m still going to be doing it because I’ve always wanted to make clothes,” he says. “It’s the only thing I am interested in.”

Amy Lawrence

“In general life, I’m quite an anxious person but I find that when I am making, I do feel calm and a lot more at ease,” says Amy Lawrence. The winner of the National Designer award in 2025 is widely regarded as one of the industry’s most exciting new talents. She works exclusively with raw silk to create the floating gowns, skirts and tops that define her eponymous label.

While Lawrence was studying at RMIT University, she came across an old-fashioned technique in a Vogue sewing manual called the faggot stitch – a ladder or lace-like way to join two pieces of hemmed fabric. She worked to evolve it from a decorative stitch into something that could work as a significant part of a garment’s construction. Her resulting pieces sit off the body, and move in a unique, otherworldly way.

In her business, every order is bespoke. They often begin with conversations via Instagram direct message. After a bit of back and forth about what the client wants, Lawrence takes their measurements at her studio in Melbourne, drafts a new pattern and makes the garment by hand. Prices start at $2,800 and range up to $7,000. She spends between 10 and 20 hours on each garment, but the turnaround time is generally dictated by the client’s needs.

Although Lawrence is exploring expanding the business to wholesale, and what it may look like to externalise some of the production process to make this feasible, it is the “slow process of making a garment”, the meditation and muscle memory of the craft, that makes her happiest.

Daniel Jones, Zink & Sons…

Source: The Guardian Life and Style | Published: 2026-11-21 19:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: What do I want from Santa? No more lazy, joyless Christmas lists | Polly Hudson
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear prose, learning value

If the first step is admitting there’s a problem, please consider this an intervention. Many of us need help, and what I’m suggesting is pretty much a cold turkey approach, no pun intended. The Christmas list must be abolished, once and for all.

It’s tricky to remember when it started, but, in my experience at least, this way of festive gifting has ramped up over the past few years, and is now threatening to become the norm. And it makes sense. Modern life is exhausting, and hard, so of course we leap gratefully onboard with anything that promises to make it easier. If a list is sent, or simply a direct link to one product, we can achieve with a few thumb movements from the comfort of the sofa what used to necessitate a journey, a fight through crowds, some searching, some queueing, and then a return journey. Instead, now, a couple of taps and a swipe, job done, lemon squeezy. But we’re not noticing what’s getting lost. On the surface we are all being given exactly what we want, but are we really?

The Christmas list process feels increasingly cold, meaningless and materialistic. If, as present-givers, we used our brains, our hearts, rather than our smartphones, maybe the gifts wouldn’t be perfect, but they’d show we’d made an effort. That we can be bothered. A deeper intention would be communicated: I know you, I get you, I’m paying attention – as opposed to: I have received your email. Meanwhile, if we’re the ones issuing instructions, the prospect of disappointment or duplication is erased, sure, but so, too, is the excitement, the anticipation, the surprise. The Russian roulette element to proceedings. The thrill of the chase.

The adults in the group I spend 25 December with – a treasured assortment of family and friends – always do Secret Santa. It started old-fashionedly, on paper, with a pen, and has become gradually more slick and technological. The person whose nine millionth festive job was wrestling with the complicated equation of who gets who found an app that does that. Brilliant. Then the app updated, to include an option for participants to add the link to a gift within the agreed budget that they’d enjoy. And naturally, if somebody you’re trying to make happy asks you for something, you give it to them.

The Secret Santa handover used to be a funny, somewhat raucous high point of the day, Santa’s representative charged with overseeing proceedings doing so with inimitable flair. The first time the app took over, it felt strangely flat. There was zero drama or intrigue. No one had been permitted to use their imagination, was worried a risk might not pay off, had the chance of pulling a maverick blinder. We needn’t have troubled ourselves with unwrapping the packages, because we all knew what was inside them already. A few years before, somebody gave me something so silly and unexpectedly touching that I laughed until I cried. There is no comparison between the two experiences, and I am factoring in the occasion when I got a stinker I donated to the nearest charity shop as soon as it reopened. Off piste is where the magic happens.

Also, it’s not like the listless have to shoot blindly into the dark. Hints can and undoubtedly will be dropped. From now until 24 December, it is impossible to go for longer than three minutes without being offered the opportunity to read a gift guide. We can ask the giftee’s friends for advice. We could turn to science – for example, the website Pebble, which analyses the psychology of the recipient and suggests ideas (with links!). We might put the recipient’s life under a thought microscope and examine it for gaps, items that would make it nicer, smoother, faster, more comfortable, fun or stylish. There are many other ways to go about this, all of which say much more about the relationship between you than any mindless mouse click ever could.

’Tis the season where you can get away with sappy cliches, like that it’s your presence, not your presents, that actually matters at Christmas, and that when it comes to shopping, it really is the thought that counts. Keep the receipt, though, obviously.

Source: The Guardian Life and Style | Published: 2026-11-22 05:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Too lazy for lawns? Try a native meadow
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, learning value

Do you yearn for that suburban dream, the perfect lawn? An instant, billiard-table smooth, weed-free, living carpet that mows and waters itself?

Do you yearn to join one of those neighbourhood groups whose members compete to show off the result – the kind of people who use laser levels and precision bombing with biological weapons to achieve grassy perfection?

Well good luck with that.

“There’s no grass that ticks all the boxes,” says Melbourne landscaper Simon McCurdy. “Each has its positive attributes and drawbacks.”

In his 38 years of experience, McCurdy has seen roll-out turf largely displace seed-sowing for lawn establishment. “Virtually all our clients want instant results,” he says. “And when you factor in the time involved in sowing from seed it’s certainly cheaper for most people to install turf.”

For larger areas McCurdy says many people choose hydroseeding, an intermediate method between seeding and turf, in which emulsions of seed, water, mulch and fertiliser are sprayed on to prepared soil. But which grass variety to choose?

“The buffalo-type grasses yellow off in winter and have an unattractive appearance,” McCurdy says. “But they self-repair and are very hardy.” On the other hand, he says fescue may look green and lush but won’t self-regenerate if it’s too dry, or when subjected to indignities by your dog.

For coastal areas McCurdy recommends kikuyu. “It’s hardy and lower maintenance and chokes the weeds,” he says. “But it’s a very strong and aggressive grass type that we wouldn’t use in a residential setting except for the nature strip, or surrounded by concrete.”

McCurdy says many of the finer-bladed, exotic species such as Santa Anna couch or Bermuda grass may look great but need high upkeep and are more suited to golf courses, where they need regular de-thatching, coring and spraying with pesticides. “You’re wasting your money and causing a headache for yourself,” he says.

So if exotic lawns can be so problematic, why don’t Australia’s lawns feature more native grass species? McCurdy can’t say, because he’s never used them. But Darren Vincent can.

Vincent is a managing director of Native Seeds, and he and his team travel Australia collecting native grass seeds, then grow, harvest and package the result on their farm in Victoria’s Ovens Valley.

Vincent recognises the business is a niche operation within Australia’s multibillion-dollar landscaping industry, and admits that growing a native lawn is more time-consuming.

“Native grass species take longer to establish because their root systems develop before showing a lot of growth above ground,” he says. “This makes them initially more vulnerable to invasion from exotics.”

But Vincent says that once established, native lawns are self-sufficient, resist introduced species, offer better drought tolerance and soil retention, and minimise or eliminate the need for fertiliser and pesticides.

Vincent supplies native lawn and flower seed to many local and state governments interested in replacing their traditional exotic lawns and gardens with low-maintenance, less thirsty native alternatives. “Councils are some of our biggest clients for getting native grasslands back into their parks and urban corridors.”

Vincent recommends native grasses for urban residential settings too, and says about 80% of his lawn products go to metropolitan Sydney and Melbourne. His meadow mix, a combination of grasses and wildflowers, is often used for Australia’s ironic icon, the “nature” strip.

“Councils only kick up if plantings on nature strips get too high,” he says. “With the right mix they’ll naturally stay within regulations.”

For those who prefer a typical, cut-grass lawn, Vincent recommends his native Griffin weeping grass, which, unlike most spring-sown exotics, germinates in autumn. “It’s indigenous to every state in Australia including coastal areas,” he says. “With irrigation over summer it will stay green all year round, is non-invasive and handles shade and salt spray well.”

Vincent dismisses concerns that native grasses, including tussock species, bring increased fire hazards. “Native species don’t have nearly as much biomass as introduced species,” he says. “Councils are turning to natives in roadside revegetation because of their reduced fire risk. And if they do burn they recover better too.”

The ecologist Dr Katherine Horsfall founded Melbourne Meadows to encourage the transformation of urban spaces with native species, and often uses examples from critically endangered grasslands and grassy woodlands.

Horsfall began her research into native meadows at the University of Melbourne’s School of Agriculture, Food and Ecosystem Sciences, and her work has led to cooperation with councils and public works contractors. Horsfall’s experiments have shown that with careful introduction, patches of mixed species-rich native plants and grasses in urban areas can provide microhabitats that encourage biodiversity and beauty.

“Victoria has lost the majority of our native grasslands and as a result many species from these ecosystems are now critically endangered,” she says. “Even small plantings help restore them.”

Horsfall tires of seeing the same plants in our suburbs. “Native meadow plantings in urban areas attract native insect and vertebrate species, and allow people to stop and reflect on nature, which has really great mental health and social outcomes.”

The other great benefit of native plantings is low maintenance – removing the need to be chained to a mower and spending big on fertilisers and potentially hazardous chemicals. And who wouldn’t rather be recreating instead?

Source: The Guardian Life and Style | Published: 2026-11-21 19:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: The moment I knew: She flew me to the scene of my favourite romantic movie
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear prose, learning value

Brianna and I met in 2013 on an arts project I was developing in Mount Druitt, the region I grew up in, in western Sydney.

It was a site-specific work for young people, and Brianna became part of the strategic leadership team, which ultimately meant she was painting gutters pink with the local kids until 9pm each night.

Our first meeting was electric – we had so much in common, I felt as if I’d been donged on the head. Through the work, I was trying to push back against the stigma of Mount Druitt and create something fun and magical, and she understood the importance of what I was trying to do. After the project, I got a position running a theatre company nearby, and I invited her on to the board.

We were both in relationships at the time and I was coming out of a deeply unhappy one. For those first two years working together, I had a secret crush on her. A few months later we were both single and I invited her over to help write a grant together for a project I hoped to do in Berlin. That week happened to be my birthday, and a friend had given me a bottle of Moët, which I planned to save for a special occasion.

At the time I had an apartment where you could sit on the rooftop overlooking the ocean. We climbed up; I remember the sun was shining brilliantly. I said: “Oh, I’ve got this bottle of Moët – would you like to have a glass?” We’ve been together ever since.

After that, I realised even more how much we had in common, even down to the little things. For example, I’ve always hated tomatoes. After lunch one day, I looked down and noticed we both had matching piles of discarded tomatoes at the side of our plates.

But one major point of difference was our attitude towards romantic movies. I’ve always loved them, particularly old ones, and went on a mission to convert Brianna. I started with my favourite classic, An Affair to Remember starring Deborah Kerr and Cary Grant. We watched it together one night, with another bottle of champagne.

There’s a scene in the movie where they get off the cruise ship and visit Cary Grant’s grandmother, Janou. I told her that when I watched it as a kid, I thought the place where they stepped off was pure magic, like when Dorothy goes to Oz.

A few months into our relationship, work sent me to Berlin, and Brianna said: “I’m coming.” Then she handed me an envelope. Inside were two plane tickets to Villefranche-sur-Mer. Where’s this? I asked. She replied: It’s the place where Deborah Kerr and Cary Grant step off the boat.

When we arrived, I couldn’t believe it. A colourful French harbour, tucked away by the Mediterranean sea. I was almost catatonic, as if I were living inside my own dream. We spent the whole week lying on the beach, watching the cruise ships sail by. With each one I would say: “Look, Cary Grant and Deborah Kerr are coming to visit us.” We stayed at a place with a spa overlooking the town and returned to the same restaurant each night to eat spaghetti with clams.

I realised then how deeply I was in love with Brianna. Taking me to my childhood dream place got to the core of who I am. It was the greatest thing anyone had ever done for me. My romantic Hollywood dream was now a part of my real-life love story.

After 10 years together, we recently got married at Clifton Gardens in Sydney. We chose it because its harbourside charm reminds us of Villefranche, and because Brianna has built a whole new love – and career – in scuba diving around those waters.

That trip to Villefranche set a precedent in our relationship: even when things get hard, we still believe in magic, and we believe in each other. Brianna has taught me how to love. We trust each other and are kind to each other – and apologise when we fall short.

Each day together is the biggest gift.

They Will Be Kings, directed and co-written by Kaz Therese, is showing on 5 February at The Edge, Federation Square, Melbourne as part of the Midsumma festival.

item.title: I’m a pro chef. Here is everything I use for stress-free Thanksgiving turkey prep
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear prose, learning value

Thanksgiving’s piece de resistance, the turkey, is a special type of stressor. It is hard to get right – that balance of juicy breast meat, crispy skin, and tender pull-apart legs and wings. But here’s what the food magazines and TV shows may not tell you: the platonic ideal of a whole roast turkey is impossible. A moist breast inhibits skin crispiness; legs cooked to succulence means the breast is cooked to dryness.

So let that be a source of relief. If a traditional roast turkey is impossible to perfect, then just control what you can. As a culinary arts and science professor, I spend my days thinking about how to make food not only tastier but smarter. Over the years, I have developed a stress-free turkey method that makes my guests happy, while allowing me to drink and schmooze rather than agonize over whether the breast is dry or whip up an 11th-hour pan gravy.

The key: I forget about serving a whole bird and prepare the turkey in pieces – butter-poached breast, legs and wings au vin, and everyone’s favorite, shards of crisp skin. Yes, you’ll lose out on the statement piece of a giant whole roast bird, but tackling it in pieces makes life much easier, and no one will complain when they turn out beautifully.

You can even avoid the trickiest part of the prep by going to a butcher or decent supermarket meat counter, where you can ask for your turkey in three sets of pieces: the boneless breast; the wings, thighs and legs; and the ribs, back and wing tips, which, along with the neck and gizzard, make great stock.

The right tools make the job even easier. You don’t need twine, a baster, a big carving fork, roasting rack or any of that noise. Below, I’ve listed my usual equipment. May the turkey part of your holiday be more relaxed and more delicious.

First, wear protection

An apron may seem like a silly affectation for a home cook. But it protects your clothes from spattering grease and, more importantly, protects your guests’ food from whatever pet hair, supermarket germs or sweater fuzzies you bring to the kitchen. I love the comfort and durability of Hedley & Bennett. They can be pricey, but if you are like me and don’t care about the color (and like surprises), they offer a mystery overstock set of three aprons at a 50% discount.

Herby, buttery turkey breast, no oven needed

This cutting board from Zwilling with the removable tray allows you to drop ingredients out of the way as you prep. Here, you can season the turkey breast in salt, pepper, herbs, garlic and plenty of butter. For carving the cooked breast later (more below), it also captures the juices. It’s marketed as a barbecue accessory, but works just as well prepping meat indoors. I like the durability of the acacia wood, but for the cost-conscious, there is a bamboo version for under $50.

Though you typically use butcher’s twine to get a roast to conform to a uniform shape, it can take some skill and practice to make it look pretty. Instead, try an easy hack: meat netting, commonly seen on hams. Just slide in your boneless, skinless turkey breasts (or a turkey roulade to be fancy) into the net and let the netting maintain the roast’s shape.

I know, sous vide sounds intimidating. But it is one of the most stress-free cooking techniques you can use. It completely removes the need for oven roasting, which risks overcooking.

With sous vide, you put your (meat-netted, liberally seasoned) turkey breast in a plastic bag with the air squeezed out. Then place the bag of turkey in a pot full of water, insert the sous vide machine, set the final temperature (I like 145F for three hours) and it is impossible to overcook. The Breville Joule is fast, works with nearly any pot and is small enough to slide into a utensil drawer when not in use. Just slice and serve.

You don’t need the fancy Thanksgiving carving set – a long thin slicing knife and an intimidating carving fork – to pull out once a year for one task. Rather, get a decent quality knife that will not only make quick work of slicing your turkey, but be your trusted companion for all your side dish prep as well. While I have expensive Japanese knives that come with my chef bona fides, I regularly go back to my $20 Mercer Santoku, which nails the balance between quality and value. It is also lightweight and comfortable, key for a long day of prep.

Dull knives are not only inefficient, but they are also dangerous and more likely to slide from food to your own flesh – leaving the turkey’s unharmed. Before you start cooking, give your knife a good sharpening. The HORL 3 rolling sharpener, which I’ve tested and reviewed for the Guardian in the past, allows anyone to easily sharpen a knife with minimal know how.

after newsletter promotion

Tender turkey au vin (the gravy is built in!)

Most oven mitts look like Mickey Mouse hands and are just about as functional when lifting something hot, heavy and greasy. What those oven mitts lack is grip. I love the Ove Glove because, unlike with a large mitten, I can grab a hot pan naturally, making it much more secure, safer and less stressful.

Traditional pan gravy, which uses pan drippings from the roast bird, is one of the most stressful things to make: because it needs to be done after the roast finishes, it inevitably competes with guest arrival and cocktail hour.

I forgo the traditional gravy in favor of a coq au vin-style turkey, made with the tail, wings, thigh and drumsticks. This means I can make the dish ahead of time: I just braise the turkey pieces in a sauce of bacon, red wine, mushroom and thyme, resulting in a rich gravy that diners can also coat the sliced breast in. I typically make it on Thanksgiving Wednesday, because like all stews, it tastes better the next day. I start with pan-searing on the stove, and finish it in a slow oven at 275F for about three hours.…

item.title: Saved for Sunday: Robert Pattinson and James Bond’s baggage problem
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear prose, learning value

The regulars

- The moment I knew: She flew me to the scene of my favourite romantic movie

- Leading questions: I’m engaged, but I can’t stop thinking about an old friend. Should I tell him how I feel?

- Stream team, Sarah’s Channel: A beauty blogger ignores the end of the world in this increasingly relatable spoof

We can’t stop talking about: Bond trading

Alyx: It has been a long road to a new Bond. Can you tell me about the speculation, and why this franchise still feels so significant?

Sian: It has been five years since Daniel Craig’s final turn as 007 (No Time to Die) was released, meaning that by the time Pattinson makes his debut (likely 2028), it will be the longest period humanity has gone without a Bond since he premiered on screen in 1962. No wonder we are so adrift in this godless maelstrom. Save us Rpatz!

The buildup has been enormous, perhaps because it is quite entertaining to have the audition process for such an iconic role play out in such a public and gossipy manner. Also, people have weirdly strong opinions about who Bond is. (Remember the fuss about Craig being blond? Remember when that was some people’s biggest problem?)

But also because this is the first time Bond is getting a proper refresh. And I am not talking about going from the camp madness of Roger Moore to gritty Timothy Dalton: Bond is now in the hands of Amazon and can maybe start shedding some of the baggage he has accumulated over the last 60-odd years.

Alyx: Talk to me about the Amazon Studios of it all …

Sian: Amazon paid $1bn for creative control over the James Bond franchise last year, taking the spy out of the hands of the Broccoli family, who steered Bond’s cinematic identity for 63 years. Some fans remain worried that Amazon, or Jeff Bezos, will ruin the franchise, with rumours of spin-offs for a teen Bond, Moneypenny and Q and even other 00s. Bezos himself clearly loves the sheen of owning Bond, saying this week that he personally reviewed several rounds of auditions and felt there was “something special” about Pattinson.

Although $1bn is an eye-watering sum, it is important to remember that Bond is hugely lucrative IP due to the overwhelming product placement that lurks in every frame. Watches, suits, booze, cufflinks, cars, shoes, phones … all of it is up for grabs. One executive involved in bidding for product placement in the first Pattinson film told the New York Times this week they have been instructed that a seven-figure offer will be needed to even get a conversation.

Alyx: Robert Pattinson makes very diverse choices as an actor. Do you think we’ll be getting the blockbuster star or the indie auteur weirdo?

Sian: Hopefully we’ll get a bit of both. Pattinson has a unique ability to straddle both worlds, having appeared in cultural juggernauts such as Harry Potter, Twilight, Batman, The Odyssey and Dune, as well as smaller projects in which he can let his freak shine, such as The Lighthouse, The Drama, Primetime, Cosmopolis, Die My Love and The Rover.

Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve has just worked with Pattinson on Dune Part III and is a big fan. None of Villeneuve’s films are laugh-a-minute affairs, but they’re usually elegant and atmospheric: the emotionally devastating Arrival, grim and thrilling Prisoners, and heart attack-inducer Sicario. Villeneuve wanted an actor who he could believe is “a killer”, with “that kind of anger deep in the eye. It’s not everybody who has that. I need someone who has that kind of unapologetic panache”. Villeneuve is a blockbuster auteur with arthouse cred – the perfect match for Pattinson.

Since Pattinson’s casting was announced, reports have emerged that the internet’s fave hot rodent boyfriend Josh O’Connor was Villeneuve’s fave Bond in the initial batch, but O’Connor later dropped out because he reportedly didn’t want the “baggage” of taking on the role. Pattinson was bought in as a late candidate and impressed Amazon so much that he managed to talk them down from a four-picture deal to three, and for more money.

Alyx: What do you most hope he’ll bring to the role?

Honestly, one genuine moment of surprise in a two-and-a-half hour film would do it for me. Pattinson is an unpredictable and interesting actor, and it feels like Bond has not been either of those things since Craig’s shower scene in Casino Royale, or his breezy flirtation with Javier Bardem in Skyfall. If he can shed the baggage O’Connor feared and do something new with the character, I’ll be happy. May it involve an alarming mouthwash technique (Primetime), or an unhinged impression of a penis (The King). Bring on the razzle dazzle.

Your week ahead

- What to watch | Catholic schoolgirls rule in “gleefully camp” coming of age horror The Body, new to Netflix. Set in 2004, it’ll give millennial viewers flashbacks, but adds a dash of satanic ritual to the trope-y teen dramas of the era.

- What to play | Possibly the most anticipated video game of all time, 13 years in the making, Grand Theft Auto VI dropped this week. It earned five stars from our games editor. She spent more than 70 hours playing it through, and says it could have taken longer, so while claims of the GTA Flu may be greatly exaggerated, you might need to take close to two weeks off to finish it.

- What to read | In Gary Shteyngart’s first book of nonfiction essays, The Sensualist, the comic novelist wants to make you feel good. Devoted to the pursuit of pleasure, from icy martinis with Gerri from Succession, to a trip to South America to meet capybaras, his adventures and style may be silly, but they’re often sharp too.

- What to cook | Cherries have arrived early this year, and they’re on special at my local grocer. While I’m happy to eat them straight by the fistful, Nigel Slater’s cherry, ginger and ricotta toasts would make a perfect weekend breakfast.…

Source: The Guardian Life and Style | Published: 2026-11-21 21:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: The 15 best holiday gift ideas readers already love – from a wiggly pillow to soft, gorgeous cashmere
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: listicle, promotional

Last week we published an exhaustive list of the 145 best holiday gifts tested, vetted and beloved by our own experts. These gifts ran the gamut from a weighted blanket and hot pot starter kit to a “Cat Crap” lip balm, to name just a few. Readers took our advice and bought everything, including the chocolate sardines to the heatable capybara plushie – but 15 items emerged as clear reader favorites. Here’s what everyone is buying this holiday season.

- Visit our ultimate holiday gift guide for obsessively vetted gift ideas, or get inspired by our full array of guides, including a gift guide for the person who has everything and a guide to cozy gifts.

Cozy Earth Stretch Knit Pyjamas

Richard Baguley, who reviews all things sleep for us, describes these pyjamas as “wonderfully cozy, with a flexible fit and a wonderful feeling of smooth luxury”.

Material Kitchen Trio of Knives

This trio of a chef’s knife, serrated knife and paring knife cover the needs of most home cooks, according to Emily Farris, a food writer. “And after more than a year of near-daily use, the Japanese steel blades on all three are still sharp.”

Buffy Wiggle Pillow

Baguley, a self-described “terrible sleeper”, said this pregnancy pillows saves him from thrashing in his sleep. “This is a perfect gift for anyone who struggles with sleep and wants to try new ways to improve it (pregnant or not).”

Material Kitchen Resting Stones

Karen Yuan, the Filter commissioning editor, said these “satisfyingly hefty pebbles make my cooking so much more convenient and delightful”. Plus, she adds, they double as minimalist home decor: “You could also use one as a tray for rings or keys.”

Anthropologie Alani Cashmere Mockneck Sweater

“Any Anthropologie employee knows about the Alani sweater,” wrote Lauren Gould, the Filter editorial coordinator. “As a former sales associate, I can attest: this bestselling cashmere style was beloved by customers and staff alike.”

Boarderie Charcuterie Board

Yuan suggests this “dazzling” charcuterie board for anyone who needs a last-minute holiday gift. With overnight shipping, it’s “nice for a host who does not need another bottle of wine as a gift, or someone far away you wish you could share a cheese plate with”.

Fly By Jing Hotpot Starter Kit

“When I’m craving hotpot but it’s too cold to venture out to a restaurant, I’ll pull this bright red set from my shelf,” writes Yuan. “Give it to a homebody who loves to cook, then wait for the hotpot dinner invite. Everyone wins!”

Leland Francis Rollerball Trio

Ricapito touts this brand founded by Dillon Peña, an Oklahoma-native makeup artist. The trio comes in three scents – El Santo (citrus and wood), La Reina (rose and herb) and Stoner (smoke and leather) – all unisex.

Bedsure Faux Fur Blanket

Chan said this is a worthy dupe for the trendy Lola blanket at a third of the price. “It’s warm and amazingly soft,” he wrote. “Like being wrapped in a teddy bear’s hug.”

Naomi After-Cooking Hand Scrub

Farris recommends this hand scrub for the “home cook who’s equally enamored with luxe smells”. Made with bread yeast enzymes to neutralize cooking odors, its bergamot and pepper scents “give off high-end hotel vibes”.

Hestra Fleece-lined Gloves

Kin Moy, a Boston-based style coach, said these are an ideal gift for a rugged guy who still loves a bit of luxury. “It manages to be really robust and sturdy.” Lauren Gould

Fishwife Gift Set

Fishwife, our reigning tinned fish taste test champion, makes a brightly illustrated gift box containing 10 bestselling tins. Gould, the Filter editorial coordinator, recommends the rainbow trout in chimichurri: “This trout blows me away with its addition of grilled red pepper and herbs.” Karen Yuan

Sezane Quarter-zip Sweater

Gould bought her (mostly) stylish 23-year-old brother this “warm and extremely comfortable” sweater. He approved.

Craftspring Oyster Ornament

Our priciest but prettiest stocking stuffer has a hand-stitched felted wool shell and a little white pearl tucked inside.

item.title: Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: promotional, off-topic

The paper fortunes of Anthropic’s seven co-founders reached a total of more than $180bn on Thursday as shares in their company started trading at a price ahead of expectations.

The opening price of $111.50 (£85) per share valued the entrepreneurs’ stakes – including the chief executive, Dario Amodei, and his sister Daniela – at between $26.5bn and $27bn each. The founders have pledged to donate 80% of their shareholdings in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, which would equate to about $150bn at the current share price.

Other investors generating considerable wealth from the float and the late share price surge include Madonna’s manager, Guy Oseary, whose venture capital firm, Sound Ventures, which he co-founded with Hollywood actor Ashton Kutcher, reportedly owns 0.5% as an early investor. That stake would be worth $10bn at the opening price.

At the closing price of $97.17, the combined co-founders’ stakes had fallen in value to just over $160bn at around $23bn each. The Sound Ventures stake was worth about $8.75bn.

Anthropic has also committed 5% of its shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, which will “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”. The company has said some of the proceeds could be used to address AI’s impact on the job market, though fears the technology will lead to significant job losses have yet to be realised.

Anthropic’s IPO is widely expected to channel vast sums into the coffers of a powerful social movement called effective altruism, via the many millions of dollars that its 5,300 staff will have made from the flotation. EA, as it is known, crystallised on university campuses in the US and UK in the early 2010s. It encourages its members to donate a substantial portion of their income to a set of specific causes that it deems high-priority. These include things like pandemic prevention, biorisk, nuclear safety and – overwhelmingly – the risks posed by advanced AI.

Anthropic’s co-founders, including Dario Amodei, are associated with EA. Amodei took a pledge to donate his income through the organisation Giving What We Can, which is associated with the movement. However, he now disavows his association and has said he does not consider himself an effective altruist.

In 2023, he told The New York Times’ Hard Fork podcast he was “sympathetic to a number of the ideas” promoted by EA, but against “dividing people up into tribes”.

Meet Anthropic’s co-founders

Dario Amodei, 43

Anthropic’s San Francisco-born chief executive was educated at Stanford and Princeton universities. He worked at the Chinese tech firm Baidu and then at Google before joining OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT and now Anthropic’s arch-rival, where he had a key position as vice-president of research.

In 2020, Amodei left OpenAI, and it has been widely reported that his departure was due to conflicting views over safety. “It is incredibly unproductive to try and argue with someone else’s vision,” he said years later.

AI safety remains a major concern for Amodei. He called for a slowdown in AI development in September after the resignation of an employee who cited concerns AI could wipe out humanity and triggered a wave of concern about the existential threat posed by the technology.

Amodei is also blunt about the potential impact of AI on jobs, claiming that AI could eliminate half of all white-collar jobs by the end of the decade.

Daniela Amodei, 39

Amodei, Dario’s sister, began her career in politics, working in Congress and on a congressional campaign, before switching to tech and taking a job at Stripe, the payment processor. She moved to OpenAI before co-founding Anthropic with her brother. She leads teams on AI model safety and alignment, making sure AI systems adhere to human aims and values.

Like other Anthropic employees and co-founders, Amodei is tied to the EA movement. She is married to one of its major donors, Holden Karnofsky, who co-founded GiveWell and the major grant-giving organisation Open Philanthropy.

Jack Clark, 38

This Brighton-born former journalist has been catapulted into the list of richest Britons with the Anthropic flotation. His paper wealth of approximately $26.6bn (£20.3bn) compares with £38bn for the London-based Hinduja brothers and puts him above the £18.2bn fortune of the Reform UK donor Christopher Harborne and Manchester United’s co-owner Jim Ratcliffe, who is worth £15.2bn. Clark leads the Anthropic Institute, a thinktank devoted to researching the social implications of advanced AI.

In a lecture at Oxford University this year, Clark predicted that an AI system will work with humans to make a Nobel prize-winning discovery within 12 months, and that tradespeople will be helped by bipedal robots within two years. He added that it would be better if humans could slow the development of the technology “to give ourselves more time as a species” to deal with the implications of its powers.

Jared Kaplan, 42

Anthropic’s chief science officer received a PhD in theoretical particle physics from Harvard before working as a researcher at OpenAI, then co-founding Anthropic. He is known for his work on scaling laws – the idea that AI models grow smarter and more powerful in proportion with the resources that are spent on training them.

In an interview with the Guardian last year, Kaplan focused on the major AI safety concern that animates much of Anthropic’s work – the power and potential risk of AI systems that can improve themselves. Creating such systems would be “the ultimate risk,” he said.

Tom Brown, 39

Anthropic’s chief compute officer, who is in charge of the company’s use and procurement of datacentres, was a senior engineer at OpenAI. Given his job title, he is unsurprisingly supportive of a divisive topic in US politics: whether to build more datacentres. Speaking in September, Brown praised Donald Trump’s social media post stating “let data reign”.…
